summary: Use the original MC6847 font for text instead of the 6847T1 glyphs
description: The port's fast text renderer (lib/coco_machine/src/coco_machine.cpp:909) hardcodes the T1 table: font_6847t1[((ch & 0x3F) | 0x40) * 12 + sub] - the UPPER 64 glyphs of the 128-glyph T1 set. Semantics were already non-T1 (uppercase-only, bit 6 = inverse via g_alpha_lut); only the GLYPH SHAPES were T1. Switching to the original MC6847 character generator restores CoCo 1 / early CoCo 2 text appearance. THREE COORDINATED CHANGES: (1) lib/xroar_core/library.json:12 explicitly excludes src/mc6847/font-6847.c from the build - that exclusion must be lifted or the symbol will not link (this is what the 'font_6847[] is a link-time stub' comment at coco_machine.cpp:756 refers to); (2) the tables differ in size AND indexing - font_6847 is 768 bytes / 64 glyphs indexed (ch & 0x3F) * 12 + sub, matching upstream mc6847.c:509, while font_6847t1 is 1536 / 128; (3) coco_machine.cpp's glyph fetch. Costs 768 bytes of flash (flash was at 1.5% of 16 MB). Behind COCO_FONT_T1 (default 0 = original 6847) so the two can be A/B'd on hardware. OUT OF SCOPE, flagged for a decision: the VDG part is still created as part_create("MC6847", "6847T1") at coco_machine.cpp:758. In upstream mc6847.c the is_t1 flag also drives bright_orange (non-T1 gets VDG_BRIGHT_ORANGE, T1 plain VDG_ORANGE, line 258), inverse_text and text_border (lines 260-261) - so switching the PART as well would change colours, not just glyphs. This issue deliberately changes the font only. Whether the port should present as a full non-T1 6847 is a separate question; the fast renderer uses its own palette, so the practical effect may be nil - verify before assuming either way. [2026-08-26 DONE - confirmed on hardware by the user] Shipped: library.json exclusion lifted; the zeroed placeholder const uint8_t font_6847[768] = {0} removed from xroar_stubs.c (it was the actual 'link-time stub', and it collided with the real table - 'multiple definition of font_6847' - the moment font-6847.c entered the build); coco_machine.cpp indexes font_6847[(ch & 0x3F) * 12 + sub] behind COCO_FONT_T1 (default 0). Health unchanged: 13.18 ms/field, 1.27x real-time, 59-60 fps, no desyncs, flash still 1.5%. RAM DROPPED ~15 KB (75.9% -> 73.0%) - unrelated to the font: the 48-entry compose ring is unreferenced in a COCO_DVI_MODE=1 build and gets garbage-collected. Remainder filed as FRUITJAM-43. [2026-08-26 FOLLOW-UP - font handling realigned to upstream] The first cut introduced COCO_FONT_T1, a SECOND independent switch: it chose the glyph table while part_create("MC6847", "6847T1") separately declared the chip, with nothing tying them together - they could disagree. Upstream has exactly one such decision: is_t1, set from the part option, selects font_6847t1 vs font_6847 inside mc6847.c (:495-509). Replaced COCO_FONT_T1 with COCO_VDG_T1 (default 0), a single source of truth feeding BOTH the part option string and the renderer's table. Indexing now taken from upstream rather than derived: non-T1 (data & 0x3f), T1 |= 0x40 then & 0x7f, both conditioned on EXT - which is tied low on the CoCo, so the external-character-generator branch never applies. Also confirmed the vendored mc6847.c is verbatim upstream apart from the one documented SUPPRESS_RENDER_SCANLINE early return, and that it includes BOTH font headers - the library.json exclusion + zeroed stub were purely this port's deviation.

summary: Decide whether the VDG part should present as a non-T1 MC6847 (colour/inverse semantics)
description: Deliberately left out of FRUITJAM-42, which changed GLYPHS only. coco_machine.cpp:758 still creates the VDG as part_create("MC6847", "6847T1"), so the port now draws original-6847 glyphs while the emulated part still identifies as a T1. In upstream mc6847.c the is_t1 flag drives three further behaviours: bright_orange (non-T1 = VDG_BRIGHT_ORANGE, T1 = plain VDG_ORANGE, line 258), inverse_text (is_t1 && (GM & 2), line 260) and text_border (is_t1 && !inverse_text && (GM & 4), line 261). WHY IT MAY BE MOOT: this port rasterises text and graphics itself (SUPPRESS_RENDER_SCANLINE) using its own g_pal palette and its own inverse handling via g_alpha_lut, so mc6847.c's render path is dead at runtime and these flags may never reach the screen. VERIFY BEFORE CHANGING ANYTHING - grep whether the fast renderer consults any is_t1-derived state, and check whether the port implements the GM&2 / GM&4 inverse-text and text-border variants at all. OUTCOME IS A DECISION, NOT NECESSARILY A CHANGE: either (a) confirm the flags are unreachable and record that, closing this, or (b) find a real difference and decide whether a CoCo 1 / early CoCo 2 presentation is wanted end-to-end. Only worth doing if someone notices a colour or border that looks wrong; low priority. [2026-08-26 RESOLVED BY VERIFICATION - no behavioural change, and the question was partly misfiled] Answer: the is_t1 flags CANNOT reach the screen in this port. Every is_t1-dependent branch in mc6847.c - font lookup, nA_S/INV decode, bright_orange, inverse_text, text_border - lives inside render_scanline() (mc6847.c:415), and the coco env compiles that function's body out via SUPPRESS_RENDER_SCANLINE (early return at :416-427). The variant is therefore inert at runtime. SECOND FINDING, the more useful one: the machine was ALREADY wired as a non-T1 6847. coco_vdg_fetch builds `v | ((v & 0xC0) << 2)` - 0x200 = A/S, 0x100 = INV - which is exactly upstream's NON-T1 decode (mc6847.c:474-478, 496). The part had been declaring itself a T1 over plain-6847 wiring since the machine was written. part_create now uses COCO_VDG_VARIANT, so the declared part matches both the wiring and the font. PROCESS NOTE: this should have been checked before being filed - one grep for the enclosing function answered it. Filing a question that a single verification closes is the same 'infer rather than check' habit that produced the wrong FRUITJAM-37 root cause.

summary: NeoPixel boot-progress indicator: red at clock/power, +green at SD mount, +blue when boot completes
description: A focused slice of FRUITJAM-16 (board UI), which stays open for buttons and the wider status/health use of the strip. Scope here is ONLY boot progress, so it can close. Three cumulative pixels on the onboard 5-NeoPixel strip (PIN_NEOPIXEL=32, NUM_NEOPIXEL=5, both already defined by the adafruit_fruitjam variant; no power gate on this rail): pixel 0 RED at boot step 0 (after vreg + set_sys_clock_khz + psram_reinit_timing); pixel 1 GREEN once the SD card mounts (step 2); pixel 2 BLUE after core 1 is launched and setup() is done. Cumulative, so the strip reads as a progress bar and a stalled boot leaves the last completed step lit - which makes it a diagnostic, not just decoration: a board that hangs on SD shows red only, a board that hangs in video init shows red+green. This complements the FRUITJAM-35 heartbeat LED (GPIO29), which covers the RUN phase; the strip covers the BOOT phase, where the heartbeat has not started yet. Uses Adafruit NeoPixel; the driver bit-bangs with interrupts disabled, which is safe here because all three writes happen before core 1 launches, and the third is the last statement in setup(). Nothing in the run loop touches the strip. KNOWN LIMITATION to check on hardware: boot is fast, so the red-only and red+green phases may be visible only as a brief flash on a healthy boot. They persist exactly as long as the step takes, which is the useful behaviour when something hangs. [2026-08-26 DONE - all five pixels, stage points chosen from MEASURED boot timing] LED 1 red power/clock (~47 ms), LED 2 amber USB host up, LED 3 green SD mounted, LED 4 cyan machine ready, LED 5 blue boot complete (~1380-1490 ms). Named constants BOOT_PIX_* rather than bare indices, since 1-based vs 0-based is exactly what gets misread here. MEASURED BOOT PROFILE, the reason the stage points sit where they do: serial-ready wait 430-520 ms with a monitor and the FULL 1500 ms without (addressed in FRUITJAM-45); SD mount 46-250 ms, varying run to run; machine init ~215 ms; audio ~299 ms; every other stage under 60 ms. Spacing is therefore approximate and honest rather than even - LEDs 2 and 3 can land close together on a fast SD mount. Deliberate: a stalled boot leaves the last completed stage lit, making the strip a boot-phase diagnostic, which the FRUITJAM-35 heartbeat LED cannot be because it only starts once loop() runs. Idle colour cycling was attempted and ships DISABLED - see FRUITJAM-47. [2026-08-26 FINAL COLOURS - confirmed on hardware] LED 1 red (255,0,0), LED 2 yellow (255,255,0), LED 3 green (0,255,0), LED 4 blue (0,0,255), LED 5 indigo (40,0,200). The indigo is TUNED FOR WS2812, not taken from sRGB: the web colour #4B0082 (75,0,130) is only 1:1.7 red:blue and reads visibly MAGENTA on these LEDs, because their red channel is perceptually stronger than the sRGB value implies. 1:5 keeps the violet cast while sitting on the blue side of it, and the brighter blue also stops LED 5 being the dimmest of the five, which #4B0082 was at setBrightness(40). Worth remembering for any future LED colour work on this board: pick by eye on the hardware, not from a hex table. [2026-08-26 LED 2 retuned to chartreuse (128,255,0)] Pure yellow (255,255,0) read too warm on these LEDs - the same WS2812 red-channel effect that made #4B0082 magenta. Tuned by eye over 255 -> 200 -> 160 -> 100 -> 128. Final palette: LED 1 (255,0,0), LED 2 (128,255,0), LED 3 (0,255,0), LED 4 (0,0,255), LED 5 (40,0,200), all under setBrightness(40). If the palette is ever revisited, the principled fix is gamma correction (Adafruit_NeoPixel::gamma32) rather than more hand-tuning: these LEDs drive PWM linearly while perception is not, which is why every colour with a mid-range channel reads hotter than its sRGB value suggests.

summary: Shorten the setup() serial-ready wait from 1500 ms to 300 ms
description: setup() blocks on `while (!Serial && (millis() - start) < 1500) delay(10)` so a serial monitor has time to attach before the boot banner prints. Measured during FRUITJAM-44: that wait is the single largest lump in boot. With a monitor attached it took 430-520 ms; with NO monitor - normal use - it runs the full 1500 ms, out of a ~1500-2600 ms boot. Nothing else happens during it. Cut to 300 ms. Saves ~1.2 s on every headless boot and makes the FRUITJAM-44 NeoPixel progression far more even, since LED 1 -> LED 2 was almost entirely this wait. KNOWN TRADE-OFF, verify on hardware: the measured attach time with a monitor was 430-520 ms, i.e. LONGER than the new 300 ms cap. So deploy.sh --capture and pio device monitor may now miss the banner and the earliest STAGE lines, because the port is not open yet when they print. That is a real cost to the diagnostic workflow - the boot log is how every hardware issue in this repo has been diagnosed. If the early lines are lost, options are: raise slightly (600 ms still saves ~0.9 s headless), or make the wait a build flag so capture builds keep the long wait while shipped firmware boots fast. Decide from what the capture actually shows, not from theory. [2026-08-26 DONE] SERIAL_READY_WAIT_MS, default 300, was a hardcoded 1500. Saves ~1.2 s on every headless boot. The predicted trade-off DID materialise and was verified both ways: at 300 ms a capture loses the banner, the serial-ready line, and the USB-host and mount-SD stages - the log opens mid-word on the tail of 'STAGE mount SD... ok'. So the value is an overridable macro, not a constant: build with -DSERIAL_READY_WAIT_MS=1500 for a complete boot log. Both paths confirmed on hardware.

summary: Detect when BASIC reaches its OK prompt (screen-based, ROM-agnostic)
description: Added basic_at_prompt(): scans the 32x16 text screen at $0400 for 'OK' at the start of any row. VDG screen codes - glyph = ch & 0x3F, and 0x00-0x1F map to '@'..'_', so 'O'=0x0F and 'K'=0x0B. One-shot from loop(); measured at 78 fields (~1.3 s) on the Disk Extended Color BASIC 1.1 config. WHY SCREEN AND NOT PC: a probe showed PC sitting in the command-input loop at $A7D3/$A7D5, a perfectly good signal - but those addresses belong to Disk Extended Color BASIC 1.1, and this port boots Color, Extended+Color or Disk depending on what is on the card. Screen text is identical in all three. MEASURED BOOT TIMELINE, kept because it is the useful artifact: f=0 screen is uninitialised 0x00 and renders as '@' everywhere; f=30-60 blank while BASIC clears RAM, PC=$A089; f=90 banner + OK present, PC=$A7D5; thereafter PC oscillates $A7D3/$A7D5 at the prompt. FOLLOW-UP WORTH TAKING: loop()'s AUTO.BIN auto-run still fires on a hardcoded 150-field timer whose comment guesses '~2.5 s'. The real signal arrives at ~78 fields, so auto-run could be about a second faster and stop being a guess. Not changed here because it alters existing working behaviour and deserves its own hardware test.

summary: NeoPixel idle colour cycle desyncs HSTX: needs a DMA-fed WS2812 writer
description: Requested: slowly cycle the strip once BASIC is up. Implemented as neo_idle_cycle() - a hue rotation with each pixel offset by a fifth of the wheel, 80 ms interval - and it works visually, but it breaks video, so it ships disabled behind NEO_IDLE_CYCLE 0. MEASURED: with the cycle on, the HSTX link desynced within ~100 fields of BASIC coming up and stayed there - 9 desync events, 8 resyncs in 14 s, video_frames at 159-161 fps instead of 60. Isolation run with the cycle off and everything else byte-identical, including the per-field screen scan: 0 desyncs, steady 59-60 fps, same detection at f=78. So the cause is show(), not the detector and not the added loop() work. CAUSE: Adafruit's RP2 backend (Adafruit_Neopixel_RP2.cpp) drives WS2812 from PIO but feeds it with pio_sm_put_blocking, spinning core 0 for ~450 us per update - 15 bytes at ~10 us each plus the reset latch - while core 1 keeps the HSTX FIFO fed. Same underrun-to-desync path as FRUITJAM-13/-37. The BOOT pixels are fine and stay enabled: all five of those writes happen before multicore_launch_core1(), so no video is streaming yet. WHY A SLOWER INTERVAL IS NOT THE FIX: the risk is per-update, not cumulative, so a rarer cycle just trades a constant glitch for a periodic one. FIX: drive the PIO SM by DMA so core 0 never spins - stage the 15-byte frame in a buffer, hand it to a DMA channel with DREQ set to the PIO TX FIFO, return immediately. The channel budget is tight and deliberately arbitrated (pico_hdmi 0/1, SD 2/3, PIO-USB 4 - see the setup() comments), so claim explicitly rather than via dma_claim_unused. Verify with a multi-minute soak counting desyncs, not a short capture: per FRUITJAM-37 the bursts are invisible in a 15 s log.

summary: Blink LED 1 during the serial-ready wait, and raise the wait to 1000 ms
description: Follow-up to FRUITJAM-45, which cut the setup() serial-ready wait from 1500 ms to 300 ms. That was too tight in practice: a monitor measured 430-520 ms to become ready, so captures lost the banner, the serial-ready line, and the USB-host and mount-SD stages - the log opened mid-word. Since the boot log is how hardware issues in this repo get diagnosed, losing its first third is a bad trade for 700 ms. TWO CHANGES: (1) default SERIAL_READY_WAIT_MS 300 -> 1000, clearing the measured attach time with about 2x margin while still saving 500 ms per boot against the original 1500; the macro stays overridable either way. (2) LED 1 now blinks red at 100 ms throughout the wait and is left solid on exit, so the longest single pause in boot reads as 'alive, waiting for a host' rather than as a possible hang - which matters more now the wait is longer again. SAFE HERE, UNSAFE LATER: driving the strip from this loop is fine because core 1 has not launched, so there is no HSTX stream for the blocking PIO write to starve. The identical call at RUNTIME desyncs video - see FRUITJAM-47. Worth keeping that contrast in mind before adding NeoPixel writes anywhere else: the boot phase and the run phase have completely different rules. [2026-08-26 DONE - confirmed on hardware] Wait raised to 1000 ms and LED 1 blinks red at 100 ms throughout, solid on exit. Full boot log is back: banner, serial-ready line, USB host and mount SD all present again. Note the wait is a CAP, not a delay - with a monitor attached it exited at 531 ms the moment Serial came ready, so 1000 vs 1500 costs an attached session nothing; only a headless boot pays the full value, and there it saves 500 ms against the original.

summary: Intermittent HSTX desync latches at boot (~1 in 4-5) and resync never recovers it
description: Split out of FRUITJAM-37, which accepted a single self-recovering desync at 1-in-589 reports and said to file separately if it recurred at a higher rate. It has. SYMPTOM: on some boots the HSTX link enters the desync state at around field 180 and STAYS there - video_frames runs at 159-161 fps instead of 60, the core-0 watchdog detects it every second and requests a resync, core 1 performs it, and it immediately desyncs again. Observed 5 desyncs / 4 resyncs in an 8 s capture with no recovery. On other boots the same binary is perfectly clean. RATE, from today's runs on the shipping DVI/native build: one 10-minute soak = 1 desync in 589 reports, self-recovered; one 10 s capture = 1 desync, self-recovered; one 8 s capture = LATCHED, no recovery; three consecutive 10 s captures of the identical binary = 0. So roughly 1 boot in 4-5 shows something, and a subset of those latch permanently. IT IS NOT THE CODE UNDER TEST: it appeared across builds differing only in a NeoPixel colour constant, which is written once at boot before core 1 launches. Reflashing the same binary produced 3 clean runs in a row. Whatever varies is not in the source. TWO DISTINCT QUESTIONS, do not conflate them: (a) why does the link desync at all, and (b) why does video_output_force_resync() fail to recover it once latched? (b) may be the more tractable and is arguably the more serious - a self-recovering glitch is cosmetic, a latched one means a broken picture until power-cycle. Note the resync path already has known cross-core hazards (see the core1_background comment in coco_main.cpp: calling force_resync from core 0 hard-locks the board, which is why it is deferred to core 1). STARTING POINTS: the ~f=180 timing is suspiciously consistent across occurrences - find what happens there (BASIC finishes its cold start at ~f=78, so it is AFTER that, not during). Instrument video_output_precomposed_stale_count / lib_resync (the [di] probe already reports them) across a latched event to see whether the library notices anything internally. Consider whether the desync predates today's work by re-testing an older commit - FRUITJAM-13 covered a 'resync freeze' and its fix was confirmed stable, so this may be a regression or may be the same bug never fully fixed. MEASUREMENT DISCIPLINE: intermittent at ~1-in-5 boots means a single clean run proves nothing. Any candidate fix needs many boot cycles, not one long soak. [2026-08-26 LIKELY SUBSUMED BY FRUITJAM-53 - check before doing any work here] This issue was filed while COCO_NEOPIXEL was effectively always on: every observation behind it - the ~1-in-4-5 boot latching, the 160 fps state, resync failing to recover - came from NeoPixel-enabled builds (a031ea2 onward). With the strip gated off, main measures 0 desyncs over 2.5 min and the user reports sustained stability. So this is probably the same bug seen before its cause was known. WHAT IS NOT EXPLAINED: FRUITJAM-37's 10-minute soak on aaa5593 - pre-NeoPixel - still showed 1 self-recovering desync in 589 reports. That residual is real and predates the NeoPixel, so do not close this issue on the strength of 53 alone. The right test is a many-boot harness on current main: if latched boots never occur, close this and keep the residual as a footnote on 37; if they still occur, this is a separate bug and 53 was only making it louder. [2026-08-26 MEASUREMENT INVALIDATED - read before trusting the bisect above] Timestamped logging shows desyncs arrive as EPISODES, not as a steady rate: on the current build, 19 consecutive resyncs one per second from 11:22:50 to 11:23:07, a straggler at 11:23:17, then quiet - and the episode began about 4 MINUTES after boot. Every bisect capture used to attribute this to the NeoPixel was 2.5-3 minutes long, so a build could measure 0 purely by ending before its first episode. The four zeros that looked like agreement may be four too-short windows. ALSO RULED OUT for that episode: no button or key activity that boot (the picker was never opened, no [btn] lines), and core 0 was idling at the BASIC prompt at 13.10 ms/field / 1.27x - not under KALEIDSC load. So the episode had no user-visible trigger and is not explained by the picker or by load. PROPER MEASUREMENT, use this and nothing shorter: scripts/serial_logger.py gives wall-clock timestamps and survives reboots. Run it for HOURS per build and compare EPISODES PER HOUR, not desyncs per 3 minutes. It also distinguishes a real desync (resync counter increments) from a sink-side dropout (counter unchanged) - the distinction that was missing for this entire investigation. ROOT CAUSE FOUND 2026-08-26 (mechanism, verified against the RP2350 datasheet and the SDK source; field measurement pending): hstx_resync() in the vendored lib/pico_hdmi/src/video_output.c was missing the RP2350-E5 workaround. E5: a DMA abort does NOT suppress the aborted channel's CHAIN_TO trigger, so the EN bit of the aborted channel AND of every channel chained to it must be cleared BEFORE the abort. hardware/dma.h documents this as the caller's job and the SDK's dma_channel_abort() does not do it - it only writes dma_hw->abort and spins on BUSY. The HSTX scanout uses DMACH_PING and DMACH_PONG chained to EACH OTHER, the worst case: aborting PING re-triggers PONG and aborting PONG re-triggers PING, so hstx_resync() left a channel LIVE while it rewrote that channel's read_addr and transfer_count and then called dma_channel_start() on it. The command stream resumes mid-word, the HSTX expander misreads every command after it, the FIFO stops back-pressuring, and the link free-runs at ~2.67x - 160 fps at 60p. That is exactly the signature in the SYMPTOM above, which means the resync could CAUSE the desync it exists to clear: the watchdog fires, the resync re-desyncs the link, the watchdog fires again a second later, and the result is the observed latch (96+ resyncs, never recovering) rather than a recovery. This also explains why the half-line 2.67x ratio SURVIVED resyncs, and why episodes appear as bursts of consecutive once-per-second resyncs. NOTE the scope limit: this explains why a desync PERSISTS and why resyncs make it worse. It does NOT explain what triggers the FIRST desync of an episode; if episodes still begin (but now recover on the first resync) the onset trigger stays open and should be re-scoped into a new issue rather than holding this one. FIX: explicit EN-clear / simultaneous-abort / EN-restore in hstx_resync(), applied to both video_output.c (built) and video_output_rt.c (not built, same defect); documented in PROVENANCE.md as the first local modification to this vendored library. The watchdog log line now prints the MEASURED fps, the frame delta and the resync ordinal, so a marginal 95 is distinguishable from a latched 160. COMPLETION CONDITION: a multi-hour capture with scripts/serial_logger.py on the NATIVE path showing either no desyncs, or desyncs that recover on the first resync (no consecutive-resync bursts), compared against the pre-fix rate in episodes per hour. MEASURED 2026-08-26, 42 min, native path, E5 fix as the only variable (docs/logs/e5-fix-native.log): 10 desync events, and ALL 10 RECOVERED ON THE FIRST RESYNC within one report period - the fps sequence after every single event is 60, 59, 59. No consecutive-resync bursts, no latch, no reboots. Compare the pre-fix behaviour recorded in docs/retrospective-2026-08-26.md: 19 consecutive resyncs one per second, and 96+ resyncs with the link stuck at 160 fps never recovering, black screen until power-cycle. The latch is gone. CLOSING at the stated symptom: 'latches ... and resync never recovers it' is fixed. NOTE the baseline is the historical record, not a re-measured pre-fix run in this session. THE REMAINDER IS FILED, not held here: onset still occurs at ~14 events/hour (FRUITJAM-58), and the 90 fps threshold misses late-in-window onsets (FRUITJAM-59).

summary: Button disk picker: browse and mount .dsk images with the three board buttons
description: The amoled port boots into a touch picker over the SD card - swipe up to open or cancel, left/right to step, tap to launch. The Fruit Jam has no picker at all: it mounts a single hardcoded /coco/dsk/AUTO.DSK (falling back to roms/coco.dsk) and that is the only disk available until you rewrite the card. This gives the three unused buttons the same job. MAPPING (button 1 = GPIO0, 2 = GPIO4, 3 = GPIO5): button 2 = previous, button 3 = next, button 1 = mount the highlighted image and close. Pressing 2 or 3 while closed opens the picker, so there is no separate open gesture. Button 1 is ALSO USB-BOOT at power-on - safe to use at runtime since BOOT is only sampled at reset, but it must never be the button a user is told to hold while power-cycling. UI: an overlay drawn straight into the 320x240 framebuffer after blit_frame(), using the VDG font the emulator already has (font_6847, 8x12 glyphs -> 40x20 character cells). No extra assets. MOUNT IS A DISK SWAP, NOT A RESET: coco_machine_mount_dsk() just swaps the image pointer and re-derives the JVC geometry, which is exactly what changing a floppy does on real hardware. Disk BASIC keeps running and DIR shows the new disk. No machine reset, so nothing in memory is lost. KNOWN RISK to watch: loading the new image reads ~160 KB from SD on core 0 mid-run, stalling the emulator for a couple of hundred ms. That is the same core-0-hogging pattern that desyncs HSTX in FRUITJAM-47, and FRUITJAM-49 shows the link can latch desynced. It is a one-off user action rather than a periodic one, so it may be tolerable - but test it repeatedly and watch for desyncs, and if it bites, read the image in chunks with yields between them. DEFERRED: autolaunch. The amoled reads DECB's own directory off the image and autotypes RUN"NAME" or LOADM"NAME":EXEC so the disk describes itself. That is the better experience and this port has the key-injection primitives (coco_machine_press_key/release_key) plus prompt detection (FRUITJAM-46) to drive it, but it is a separate piece of work - this issue is browse-and-mount only so it can close. CLOSING 2026-08-26, overdue: this shipped in 299f67e and merged to main in a1bb29b, and has since been extended and re-verified on hardware several times over - FRUITJAM-66 (halt while open, button remap), -68 (ESC cancel), -69 (mount + cold boot), -70 ([CANCEL] row). It was left 'in-progress' by oversight while work built on top of it. Both input paths are confirmed working on hardware: buttons browse and mount with no keyboard attached, and F12/arrows/ENTER do the same.

summary: Keyboard control for the disk picker: F12 toggles, arrows move, Enter mounts
description: Doubles up the FRUITJAM-50 button picker with keys, so either input works at any time. F12 opens the overlay and cancels it, UP/DOWN move the selection, ENTER mounts and closes. Handled at the top of hid_keyboard_apply(), before the key-matrix diff, for the same reason as the existing Ctrl+Alt+Del reset chord: so the keys never leak through into BASIC. The overlay is MODAL while open - every key is swallowed, not just those four - otherwise the user would be typing into BASIC behind an overlay they are reading, unable to see the result. Opening it also calls coco_machine_release_all_keys() and clears the matrix state, since a key held at the moment F12 arrives would otherwise stay stuck down for as long as the picker is up. summary: Runtime PSRAM/QMI traffic makes the HDMI sink lose lock while our stream stays correct
description: Two independently-reported symptoms converge on one factor. (1) Mounting a disk from the FRUITJAM-50 picker turns the screen black. (2) Running LOADM off a mounted disk loses sync. The first WRITES ~160 KB into PSRAM; the second READS sectors out of the disk image in PSRAM via the emulated FDC. Neither touches the rendering path. PROVED NOT TO BE OUR RENDERING: instrumented immediately after a mount that blacked the screen - PC=$A7D3 (BASIC idling healthily at its prompt), screen RAM intact with the full banner and OK prompt, and fb_nonblack=768/768, i.e. every sampled pixel of the framebuffer's active area painted. The image is fully rendered and being transmitted; the monitor is not showing it. ALSO NOT VISIBLE TO OUR WATCHDOG: throughout, video_frame_count advanced at exactly 60 fps (9 frames across a 150 ms mount), the desync watchdog never fired, and pico_hdmi's own counters stayed at stale=0 / lib_resync=0. So whatever happens corrupts the SIGNAL without disturbing the command stream or the frame cadence - which is why every log looked clean while the user was staring at a black screen. TWO CANDIDATE MECHANISMS, not yet distinguished: (a) QMI contention - PSRAM and XIP flash share the QMI, so heavy PSRAM traffic stalls any video code still fetched from flash. Note the scanline ISR and our callback ARE RAM-resident (__scratch_x / RAM_FUNC), which argues against this and makes it worth checking what else on core 1 is not. (b) Supply or ground noise from sustained QMI activity degrading TMDS signal integrity enough for an already-marginal sink to drop lock. (b) fits the evidence better - it explains corruption with a correct command stream - but is much less pleasant, since firmware can only spread the traffic, not eliminate it. DONE SO FAR: load_psram_file() now reads in 4 KB chunks instead of one large burst, which should help the MOUNT case. It does nothing for LOADM, where the FDC reads sectors from PSRAM as the emulated program runs. DECISIVE NEXT TEST: drive heavy PSRAM reads from a timer with no disk and no SD involved, and see whether the sink drops lock. That separates 'PSRAM traffic' from 'disk activity' in one run. If PSRAM is confirmed, options are sector caching in SRAM, streaming disk sectors straight from SD instead of staging the image in PSRAM, or accepting it and documenting the limit. RELATED: docs/psram-policy.md already calls PSRAM 'poison in the per-frame hot path' but only on THROUGHPUT grounds (~10 MB/s, a framebuffer copy eats a frame). This is a different and undocumented hazard - PSRAM traffic costing the SINK's lock - and the policy should say so once confirmed. MAY SUBSUME OTHER ISSUES: FRUITJAM-49 (intermittent latched desync) and possibly the residual flakiness behind FRUITJAM-37 could be the same underlying problem seen from different angles. Do not close either on the strength of this one until that is actually tested. [2026-08-26 CLOSED - hypothesis DISPROVED by its own test] Built the isolation test: 5 s of heavy PSRAM reads alternating with 5 s of none, no SD and no disk activity, only PSRAM bus traffic varying. The user watched the screen and sync loss did NOT follow the 5 s boundaries. PSRAM is exonerated. The real cause was found by bisection - see FRUITJAM-53. The mount and LOADM symptoms that motivated this issue were coincidence: the link was desyncing roughly once a minute regardless, so whatever action was in progress looked causal. KEPT: load_psram_file() reads in 4 KB chunks rather than one 160 KB burst - written for this non-bug, harmless, mildly good practice, so it stays.

summary: NeoPixel begin() holds a PIO state machine and costs ~15 HSTX desyncs per 3 minutes
description: Found by bisection after the user reported sync going in and out repeatedly. BISECT, 3-minute captures counting '! HSTX desync': aaa5593 (the DVI fix, pre-NeoPixel) = 0; 1525a48 (fonts, still pre-NeoPixel) = 0; main with the NeoPixel calls disabled and everything else identical = 0; main as committed = 15. a031ea2 is the commit that introduced it. MECHANISM: Adafruit_NeoPixel::begin() calls rp2040claimPIO(), which claims a PIO state machine for GPIO32 via pio_claim_free_sm_and_add_program_for_gpio_range and HOLDS it for the life of the object. The claim happens early in setup() and was never released. Note this DISPROVES the reasoning recorded on FRUITJAM-47, which argued the boot pixels were safe because all five writes complete before multicore_launch_core1(). The writes do - the PIO claim does not. PARTIAL FIX APPLIED: the strip is now heap-allocated and deleted before core 1 launches (~Adafruit_NeoPixel calls rp2040releasePIO()), and GPIO32 is driven low afterwards rather than left floating into five WS2812 data inputs. That took 15 -> 3 in one run, but a near-identical rerun gave 14, so it is NOT established as a fix. MEASUREMENT PROBLEM, do not repeat it: this fault is boot-latched with high variance - a boot either latches at 160 fps and stays, or runs clean - so single 3-minute A/B runs cannot distinguish a partial fix from noise. Only the four zeros above are trustworthy, because they agreed across different builds. Any candidate fix needs MANY BOOT CYCLES, counting latched vs clean boots, not one long capture. SHIPPED STATE: COCO_NEOPIXEL build flag, default 0 (strip off), verified 0 desyncs. Set to 1 to get the FRUITJAM-44 boot progress bar back and accept the current instability. TO FIX PROPERLY, pick one: (a) establish whether release-before-core1 is genuinely sufficient, using a many-boot harness; (b) find out WHICH PIO gets claimed and whether it collides with PIO-USB - GPIO32 needs a PIO gpio_base of 16 while PIO-USB on GPIO1/2 needs 0, and gpio_base is per-PIO-block, so an ordering collision is plausible and would also explain why releasing the SM does not fully restore things (unclaiming does not restore gpio_base); (c) drop the library and bit-bang WS2812 at boot, which needs no PIO at all and leaves nothing behind. (b) is the most informative and cheapest to check first. [2026-08-26 CORROBORATED] User reports sustained stable HDMI since flashing 8ca9872 (COCO_NEOPIXEL=0) - a far longer clean window than any of the 2.5-3 minute captures used to bisect, and the strongest single piece of evidence that the NeoPixel PIO claim was the cause. [2026-08-26 MEASUREMENT INVALIDATED - read before trusting the bisect above] Timestamped logging shows desyncs arrive as EPISODES, not as a steady rate: on the current build, 19 consecutive resyncs one per second from 11:22:50 to 11:23:07, a straggler at 11:23:17, then quiet - and the episode began about 4 MINUTES after boot. Every bisect capture used to attribute this to the NeoPixel was 2.5-3 minutes long, so a build could measure 0 purely by ending before its first episode. The four zeros that looked like agreement may be four too-short windows. ALSO RULED OUT for that episode: no button or key activity that boot (the picker was never opened, no [btn] lines), and core 0 was idling at the BASIC prompt at 13.10 ms/field / 1.27x - not under KALEIDSC load. So the episode had no user-visible trigger and is not explained by the picker or by load. PROPER MEASUREMENT, use this and nothing shorter: scripts/serial_logger.py gives wall-clock timestamps and survives reboots. Run it for HOURS per build and compare EPISODES PER HOUR, not desyncs per 3 minutes. It also distinguishes a real desync (resync counter increments) from a sink-side dropout (counter unchanged) - the distinction that was missing for this entire investigation. LIKELY EXPLAINED 2026-08-26 by FRUITJAM-75. The bisect that produced 0/0/0/15 across builds never had a mechanism for how NeoPixel init could cost HSTX stability. Code layout is one: each build in that bisect had a different flash layout for core 0's per-field path, which is now measured to swing the desync rate by three orders of magnitude on its own. Re-run against a layout-immune build (FRUITJAM-76) before treating the NeoPixel claim as real. RE-TESTABLE 2026-08-27 by FRUITJAM-76: a bisect now means something, because builds no longer differ by layout. Re-run the NeoPixel comparison before treating the 0/0/0/15 result as real. RE-MEASURED AND DISPROVED 2026-08-27 on the layout-immune build. THE STATED MECHANISM IS WRONG. Three arms, same board, same morning, machine idle throughout: COCO_NEOPIXEL=1 (code present, strip lit) 29.1 min, 10 desyncs = 20.6/hr. COCO_NEOPIXEL=0 (code absent, strip STILL LIT because WS2812s latch and a reset does not clear them) 11.3 min, 4 desyncs = 21.2/hr. Overnight reference (code absent, strip DARK) 5.38 hr, 32 desyncs = 5.9/hr. The two lit arms are indistinguishable at ~21/hr whether or not the NeoPixel code is compiled in, so begin() holding a PIO state machine costs NOTHING measurable - the GPIO32/gpio_base-16 collision hypothesis with PIO-USB is not supported. What the rate tracks is ILLUMINATION: ~21/hr lit vs ~5.9/hr dark, roughly 3.5x. Five WS2812s draw ~50-100 mA, and rail noise next to a marginal TMDS link is the plausible mechanism. THE ORIGINAL OBSERVATION WAS REAL, THE EXPLANATION WAS NOT - enabling NeoPixels lit the strip, and that is what cost stability. The magnitude was also overstated by ~15x: this issue claims ~15 desyncs per 3 minutes (~300/hr); measured is 20.6/hr. The 0/0/0/15 bisect it rested on is uninterpretable for the reason recorded above (FRUITJAM-75: those builds differed in layout, which alone swings the rate by three orders of magnitude). CAVEAT, stated because it was not measured: the same-session LEDs-dark arm was started and then deliberately cut short at the user's request, so the dark figure is the overnight run rather than a same-morning control. The two lit arms ARE same-morning and agree with each other. DECISION (user, 2026-08-27): the strip should stay lit; the boot progress LEDs are wanted and the ~15/hr is accepted. COCO_NEOPIXEL now defaults to 1 again, restoring the pre-FRUITJAM-53 behaviour including the red flash at startup. The cost is recorded at the flag so it is a choice rather than an accident. Closing as disproved.

summary: Ship the classic scanout path: desyncs recover instead of latching the screen black
description: Does NOT fix the desync - that is FRUITJAM-49, still open. It changes the FAILURE MODE, which on this hardware is the difference between usable and not. OBSERVED, same session, same board, same sink: native_pixel_mode latched permanently - 96+ resyncs, link stuck at 160 fps, video_output_force_resync() never recovering, black screen until power-cycle. Classic path: 32 resyncs over 12.6 minutes, each a brief flicker, clean in between, still running. MECHANISM (consistent, not proven): native_pixel_mode swaps the scanout DMA channel between 16- and 32-bit control EVERY LINE (video_output_rt.c:1116). If that swap gets out of step, command lists go out at the wrong width and lines halve - and 160 fps is 2.67x of 60, exactly the half-length-line ratio, the same signature seen when init used a 320-wide mode during FRUITJAM-37. A resync can re-enter the same state, so it never escapes. The classic path never changes width, so the resync restores it. NO PERFORMANCE COST: 13.10 ms/field classic vs 13.19 native, both 1.27x real-time. This CORRECTS an earlier claim in FRUITJAM-37 that the classic path burned headroom down to 1.04x - that reading was wrong, the 16 ms was FRUITJAM-38's step, which occurs on any build regardless of scanout path. COST: the per-line copy runs on core 1 instead of a pointer handoff. Core 1 has ample headroom (docs/dual-core.md: near-zero CPU) and the measurement above shows no core-0 impact. REVISIT IF: FRUITJAM-49 finds the real cause, or the compose ring is ever needed - HDMI audio (FRUITJAM-14) requires the precomposed path, so this choice and that feature interact. CORRECTION 2026-08-26 (two): (1) the citation 'video_output_rt.c:1116' is to a file that is NOT COMPILED - lib/pico_hdmi/library.json excludes video_output_rt.c and the built implementation is video_output.c. The mechanism described is real and does exist in the built file, at video_output.c:628, where native_pixel_mode swaps al1_ctrl between dma_ctrl16 and dma_ctrl32 per line; only the line reference was wrong. (2) FRUITJAM-49 has since found a better explanation for the native-vs-classic difference: hstx_resync() was missing the RP2350-E5 abort workaround, so a resync could re-desync the link. That is a stronger cause than the width swap and, if it holds up in measurement, this issue's premise - that the two paths fail differently - may not survive. HELD, still uncommitted; the patch is parked at scratchpad/fruitjam-55-classic-path.patch. Do NOT land it until the E5 fix has been measured alone, or the two changes cannot be told apart. REVISIT TRIGGER: the E5 measurement completes. CLOSED 2026-08-26, superseded. Its premise was that native latches and classic recovers. After the FRUITJAM-49 E5 fix the NATIVE path recovers on the first resync in 10 of 10 measured events, so there is no failure-mode difference left to buy and no reason to give up the pointer handoff or the compose ring that FRUITJAM-14 needs. The parked patch is at scratchpad/fruitjam-55-classic-path.patch. REVISIT IF: FRUITJAM-58 finds an onset cause specific to the native width swap.

summary: hstx_resync() leaves the HSTX pins live across the restart, forcing the sink to re-acquire
description: Found while root-causing FRUITJAM-49. The BUILT scanout implementation, lib/pico_hdmi/src/video_output.c, touches the HSTX GPIOs exactly once, at init (video_output.c:820). hstx_resync() never touches them: it aborts the DMA, clears HSTX_CTRL_CSR_EN (which resets the shift register and clock generator), re-enables HSTX and restarts the DMA - all with the pins still driven by HSTX. The sink therefore sees the TMDS clock stop and restart mid-garbage and must fully re-acquire, typically 0.5-2 s of black, EVERY time the watchdog fires. The UNBUILT video_output_rt.c does this correctly and is the reference: it parks the pins to GPIO_FUNC_SIO before disabling HSTX (its step 2, 'no garbage on pins'), and after restarting it WAITS for the first valid line to serialize before reconnecting them (its steps 9-10, 'TV sees valid TMDS immediately'). Port those two steps into video_output.c's hstx_resync(). Note the same omission exists in video_output.c's INIT path, which connects the GPIOs at :820 BEFORE dma_channel_start() at :866, where rt.c waits first - worth fixing in the same change. DELIBERATELY NOT bundled with the FRUITJAM-49 E5 fix: this repo has been burned by changing two things and being unable to attribute the result, so the E5 fix is measured alone first. REVISIT TRIGGER: do this once the E5 fix has a measured episodes-per-hour number to compare against. COMPLETION CONDITION: hstx_resync() parks and restores the pins, and a capture shows resync events producing a brief flicker rather than a multi-second black drop-out.

summary: Desync watchdog has no backoff: it re-fires every second and can outpace sink re-acquisition
description: The core-0 desync watchdog in src/coco/coco_main.cpp fires whenever the once-per-second report measures fps > 90, with no rate limit, no backoff and no check that the previous resync helped. A sink needs roughly 0.5-2 s to re-acquire after an HSTX restart (see FRUITJAM-56), so a watchdog that restarts the link once a second can prevent the sink from ever completing acquisition - the observed '19 consecutive resyncs, one per second' and '96+ resyncs, never recovering' are both consistent with the recovery action outpacing the recovery. Proposed: after requesting a resync, hold off for N report periods before requesting another; escalate the hold-off if the link does not return to ~60 fps; and after K failed attempts stop resyncing altogether and log that, on the grounds that a stable wrong stream is more likely to be re-acquired than one that is restarted every second. Also consider a shorter detection window than 1 s so onset is caught sooner. DEFERRED, not rejected: FRUITJAM-49's E5 fix may remove the need entirely, because with E5 fixed a resync should actually work and the burst behaviour should disappear. REVISIT TRIGGER: file measurement after the E5 fix still shows bursts of consecutive resyncs. COMPLETION CONDITION: either the E5 measurement shows no consecutive-resync bursts and this closes as unnecessary, or backoff is implemented and a capture shows resync attempts spaced far enough apart for the sink to re-acquire. CLOSED 2026-08-26 by its own completion condition: the E5 measurement showed NO consecutive-resync bursts (10 isolated events in 42 min, all recovering on the first resync), so backoff is unnecessary - with E5 fixed the resync actually works. The detection-window half of this issue is re-scoped into FRUITJAM-59.

summary: What TRIGGERS an HSTX desync onset? Still ~14 events/hour after the E5 fix
description: The remainder of FRUITJAM-49, which fixed why a desync PERSISTS (RP2350-E5 in hstx_resync()) but not what STARTS one. Measured after that fix: 10 events in 42 minutes on the native path, roughly 14 per hour, each now a brief flicker that recovers on the first resync rather than a latch. Onset is therefore a separate fault and needs its own hunt. EVIDENCE ALREADY IN HAND from docs/logs/e5-fix-native.log: the caught fps values are 123, 133, 139, 142, 147, 157, 159, 159, 159, 160 - not a uniform 160. A window that reads 133 means the link ran at 60 for part of the second and ~160 for the rest, so these are ONSET windows and the fraction gives a sub-second estimate of when onset happened inside the window. Intervals between events were 18 s to 13 min with no obvious periodicity. STILL-UNTRIED LEADS, carried from the retrospective: the cold-boot test (behaviour degraded across a long session in a way no code change explains, on a board running for hours at 252 MHz with vreg at 1.25 V); many boot cycles rather than one long run, since boot-latched faults need boot cycles; and correlating onset against PSRAM/QMI, SD and USB activity. COMPLETION CONDITION: a named trigger for onset supported by a multi-hour or many-boot capture, or a measured change in events per hour from a single-variable experiment. REFRAMED 2026-08-26 by FRUITJAM-75: desync rate is driven by core-0 CODE LAYOUT in flash, not by how much work core 0 does. 110 lines of never-executed code took the rate from 0/hr to 964/hr. The 'rate tracks core-0 headroom' hypothesis recorded above is CONFOUNDED - avg run itself moves with layout. Any onset experiment must first make the hot path layout-immune (FRUITJAM-76) or the act of adding instrumentation changes the thing being measured. EVIDENCE AGAINST THE DEGRADATION HYPOTHESIS, 2026-08-27. The retrospective's leading theory was that behaviour degrades across a long session - 'no code change explains that trajectory', board running for hours at 252 MHz with vreg at 1.25 V - and a cold-boot test was named the highest-value next step. The FRUITJAM-75 confirmation run contradicts it: 3.3 hours continuous on a board already powered for 9+ hours, the rate IMPROVED, 45/hr over the first 49 minutes then 13.0/hr over the following 148 minutes, with 0 reboots and avg run flat. Degradation over a session is not supported. The trajectory the retrospective observed is better explained by FRUITJAM-75: those sessions were rebuilding and reflashing repeatedly, and each build had a different core-0 code layout, which is now measured to swing the rate by three orders of magnitude on its own. The cold-boot test is correspondingly LOWER value than recorded; the layout-immunity work (FRUITJAM-76) should come first. UNBLOCKED 2026-08-27 by FRUITJAM-76: the per-field path is now layout-immune (adding 96 lines of dead code moves avg run by 0.3%, against 12% before), so instrumentation can be added without changing the rate being measured. Onset can now be hunted properly. Current idle rate on the layout-immune build is 13/hr. CLEAN BASELINE ESTABLISHED 2026-08-27 (docs/logs/fj76-F-ballast.log, from the 02:05:21 reboot): 5.38 hours on the layout-immune build, 5815 reports, 32 desyncs = 5.9/hr, 0 reboots, machine idle throughout (no non-ROM PCs sampled). avg run held 11947-12685 us all night. This is the lowest sustained rate the project has recorded and the first baseline taken on a build where adding instrumentation does not itself move the number - so it is the reference any onset experiment should now be compared against. Hourly counts 7, 3, 4, 7, 10, 1 show NO trend across 5.4 hours on a board powered ~15 hours, which is a third independent contradiction of the session-degradation theory. NEXT STEPS, now actually measurable: instrument onset directly (what changes in the 150 ms before a desync), and re-run FRUITJAM-53's NeoPixel comparison against this baseline. LOAD MEASUREMENT ATTEMPTED AND WITHDRAWN 2026-08-27. An idle-vs-load comparison was derived by segmenting one continuous log on inferred machine state (PC below $8000 taken to mean a program was running) and written up as 31.5/hr idle vs 49.0/hr under load. WITHDRAWN: the segmentation was inference, not a controlled experiment - the log was not recorded with the arms defined in advance, nobody was managing the board, and the reconstructed timeline did not match the user's account of what was actually running. PC sampling proved unreliable for this twice in the same session, once flagging a machine as busy on a single non-ROM sample out of 1751. HOW TO DO IT PROPERLY, since the question is still open and worth answering: define the arms first, flash separately, run each for an hour or more with nothing else touching the board, and do not segment a single log by inferred state. NOTE the noise floor that makes this necessary: idle in an identical configuration measured 20.6, 21.2 and 31.5/hr across ~20-minute windows, so a 50% spread is ordinary and no short window can resolve a load effect. STANDING BASELINE 2026-08-28 (docs/logs/fj82-samprobe.log): 25.2 hours, 21,141 reports, 191 desyncs = 7.6/hr, strip LIT and mixed load throughout (idle, demo running, user testing). The 12 reboots in that window were user reflashes and resets, not firmware faults. Compare 964/hr at the FRUITJAM-75 low point and 5.9/hr for the overnight dark-idle run. THIS IS THE NUMBER TO BEAT - any future change should be measured against 7.6/hr over a comparable window, not against the shorter 20-40 minute figures from 2026-08-27, which sit inside a noise floor of 20.6-31.5/hr for identical configurations.

summary: Desync watchdog's 90 fps threshold over a 1 s window misses late-in-window onsets
description: Found in the FRUITJAM-49 measurement. The watchdog computes fps over the once-per-second report window and fires above 90. Because a desync free-runs at ~160, a window that straddles onset reads somewhere between 60 and 160 in proportion to when onset happened: the captured values include 123, 133, 139, 142 and 147. An onset in the LAST few percent of a window therefore reads close to 60 - e.g. onset at 95 percent gives about 65 fps - and slips under the 90 threshold entirely, so the fault is not caught until the NEXT window, adding up to a full extra second of desynced output. Consistent with the capture, where four events read a clean 159/160 (a window wholly inside a desync) rather than an intermediate onset value. FIX DIRECTION: sample video_frame_count on a shorter cadence than the 1 s serial report - the detection logic does not need to be tied to the report interval - so onset is caught within roughly 100-250 ms. COMPLETION CONDITION: detection latency measurably reduced, shown by captured fps values clustering near 160 (a short window wholly inside the fault) instead of spreading across 120-160. CONFIRMED AND FIXED 2026-08-26. Observed live under KALEIDSC: 13:35:31 reads 59 fps, 13:35:32 reads 81 fps (a real desync second, MISSED because 81 < 90), 13:35:33 reads 159 and fires, 13:35:34 back to 60. A 2 s blank of which a FULL SECOND was the watchdog not noticing. Six such missed windows across the log: 68, 71, 71, 74, 81, 83 fps. FIX: detection moved out of the 1 s serial report into its own 150 ms sampler in loop(); the 1 s check is kept as a backstop. 150 ms not 100 ms for margin - healthy delivers 9 frames per window vs 24 desynced, so the >90 threshold at 13.5 frames clears sampling jitter comfortably, and a false positive is expensive because a needless resync is itself a visible dropout. A 400 ms hold-off after firing stops redundant requests while core 1 performs the resync asynchronously. Expected effect: blanks halve, from ~2 s to ~1 s plus sink re-acquisition; FRUITJAM-56 addresses the re-acquisition half.

summary: Emulator liveness probe: PC, field-sync IRQ rate and VDG-buffer hash once per second
description: Filed after a KALEIDSC freeze that the existing instrumentation could not explain. The screen was frozen while every counter we had read perfectly healthy: 0 reboots, field counter climbing unbroken past 159,000, video at 60 fps, avg run steady. A hung EMULATOR and a stuck EMULATED PROGRAM are indistinguishable from fields/fps alone - this is the same class of mistake as 'a clean serial log means transmitting, never displaying' in the retrospective, one level up the stack. The only clue was that avg run stepped 16,040 -> 16,590 us at the moment it died: that figure is host time for a FIXED 14,915 emulated cycles, so it moves only when the 6809 INSTRUCTION MIX changes, which suggested a spin rather than a clean exit. Suggestive, not conclusive, and there was no way to confirm it. coco_machine.h already exposed coco_machine_get_pc(), get_irq_count() and peek_ram(); none was wired to anything. ADDED to the once-per-second report: PC (pinned or narrowly oscillating = the 6809 is SPINNING, not that we are hung), irq/s (field-sync IRQs taken, ~60 healthy, 0 = interrupts masked by CWAI/SYNC or a crash leaving F/I set), and a hash of the 24 KB VDG buffer sampled every 4th byte (unchanged across 5+ seconds prints '! SCREEN STATIC'). Cost is a few thousand cycles once per second, far under the noise floor of a 16 ms field - which matters because core 0 is at 1.01x real-time under load. KNOWN-GOOD BASELINE captured at first run: PC=$A089 irq/s=59 during BASIC's boot RAM clear, then PC=$A7D3 irq/s=60 at the idle prompt, matching the idle PC the retrospective recorded. NOTE $A7D3 pinned with irq/s=60 and a static screen is NORMAL (sitting at the prompt); a crash should show a different PC. COMPLETION CONDITION: the next freeze is captured with this probe running and classified as one of spinning 6809 / masked interrupts / program idle-by-design.

summary: Crop the VDG border and scale the active area 2.5x to fill 640x480 (COCO_CROP_BORDER)
description: The default path centres the CoCo's 256x192 active area in a 320x240 framebuffer and lets scanout double it, so the picture occupies 512x384 of 640x480 with a 64/48 px border. That border is FAITHFUL - the real VDG draws one - but it costs 44% of the screen area. Cropping makes the arithmetic exact rather than messy: 640/256 and 480/192 are both 2.5, so the active area alone fills the screen with aspect preserved. TRADE-OFF ACCEPTED: 2.5 is non-integer, so source pixels alternate 2 and 3 output pixels wide (the 2,3,2,3 pattern), which on text shows as uneven stroke weight within a glyph - an 8px cell becomes 20px with strokes of 2 and 3 px. Judged tolerable because the sink ALREADY resamples 640x480 to the panel non-integrally, so this SUBSTITUTES for the first scaling stage rather than adding one. IMPLEMENTATION exploits an asymmetry: vertical scaling is free, horizontal is not. Vertical is pure row selection - g_row[] maps 480 output lines onto 192 source rows, one load in the scanline callback, no per-pixel cost. Horizontal is fixed by HSTX (expand_shift ENC_N_SHIFTS=2/ENC_SHIFT=16: one 32-bit word always feeds two pixels, an active line is always 320 words); the default path's free 2x comes from native_pixel_mode's 16-bit reads BUS-REPLICATING each halfword, so turning native_pixel_mode OFF makes those same 320 words carry 640 DISTINCT pixels - 1:1, still a pure pointer handoff, still zero per-line CPU on core 1. VERIFIED in the built video_output.c: video_output_handle_active_start() checks scanline_pointer_callback first and unconditionally, before it looks at dvi_mode. So the buffer is 640 wide but 192 tall. The blit exploits a second alignment: one packed VDG byte is two pixels and 2.5x turns two pixels into five, so the nibble pair and the 2,3 pattern coincide - 128 iterations per row instead of 256, halving loop count while raising stores 2.5x. COST: RAM goes 73.4% -> 91.3% (384,588 -> 478,660 bytes), leaving only ~45 KB for heap and stack against ~139 KB today. That is the main risk and it is UNVERIFIED at runtime - SD, FatFS and TinyUSB all allocate. OFF BY DEFAULT behind COCO_CROP_BORDER pending measurement, because the other cost is core-0 blit time and core-0 headroom is the variable that correlates with desync rate (FRUITJAM-58). A [blit] us/field probe was added to both paths to make the comparison directly. COMPLETION CONDITION: [blit] measured on both paths, a runtime check that the reduced heap does not break SD/USB, and a decision to flip the default or not. MEASURED AND DECIDED 2026-08-26, all four on the same board back to back (docs/logs/fj61-*, fj62-*): border 2x blit 3137 us / avg run 13244 us / 1.26x / RAM 73.4%; crop HARD 2358 / 12435 / 1.34x / 91.3%; crop EDGE-BLEND 2654 / 12690 / 1.31x / 91.4%; crop FULL LINEAR 4175 / 14247 / 1.17x / 91.7%. TWO RESULTS WORTH KEEPING. (1) The cropped path is FASTER than the shipping default - 2654 us vs 3137 us - despite drawing 2.5x the output pixels. The cause is the inner loop, not the scaling: the default blit runs 256 iterations per row and does a nibble select PER PIXEL, while the cropped blit runs 128 and extracts both nibbles once per byte. Halving the loop count and hoisting the nibble extract beats 2.5x the stores. This refutes the assumption the issue was filed on, that cropping would cost core-0 time. (2) Edge blending (COCO_CROP_SMOOTH=2, blend only the shared boundary pixel) costs +296 us where full linear interpolation costs +1817 us - about a sixth of the price - because it targets the actual defect, uneven stroke weight, rather than softening edges that were already correct. DECISION: default stays border 2x (COCO_CROP_BORDER=0). User reviewed all three on hardware: the cropped edge-blend picture was judged good, with fuzziness confined to FONTS - expected, since font strokes are 1 px wide at maximum contrast, where a 50/50 boundary blend is proportionally most visible, while bitmap graphics have longer colour runs that hide it. Crispness on text won over screen area. The cropped path is kept, working and measured, behind the flag. CLOSING at that: the path exists, is characterised, and the default is chosen. REVISIT TRIGGER for anyone turning COCO_CROP_BORDER on: RAM goes to 91.4%, leaving ~45 KB for heap and stack against ~139 KB - it BOOTS and runs, but SD and USB enumeration under the reduced heap were never verified (the one-keypress check is F12 for the disk picker, which exercises both plus the overlay's 2.5x column mapping). Remainder filed as FRUITJAM-63.

summary: Rewrite the default 2x blit byte-at-a-time to drop the per-pixel nibble select
description: Incidental finding from FRUITJAM-61, and it applies to the SHIPPING path regardless of whether cropping is ever enabled. blit_frame()'s default branch loops 256 times per row and recomputes the nibble select for every pixel: idx = (x & 1) ? (src[x>>1] >> 4) : (src[x>>1] & 0x0F), so each pixel pays a shift and a branch plus a redundant re-read of the same byte. The cropped path showed the fix by accident - read one byte, extract both nibbles once, emit both pixels - and measured 2654 us against the default's 3137 us while writing 2.5x AS MANY PIXELS. The default can have the same treatment: per byte, one read, two palette lookups, then a,a,c,c for the 2x duplication, 128 iterations per row instead of 256. Expected saving is most of the ~800 us gap, i.e. roughly 3137 -> ~2400 us/field. WHY IT MATTERS beyond tidiness: core-0 headroom is the variable that tracks HSTX desync rate (FRUITJAM-58), measured at 13.0 ms -> 15 desyncs/hr against 16.0 ms -> 25/hr, and the board sits at 1.01x real-time under KALEIDSC. ~700 us/field is real headroom bought for a loop rewrite with no behavioural change. COMPLETION CONDITION: default-path [blit] measurably below 3137 us/field with the rendered output unchanged - verify by comparing a VDG-buffer hash, or simply by eye against the current build.

summary: F11 to toggle zoom (border 2x <-> cropped 2.5x) at runtime
description: DEFERRED by decision 2026-08-26, not rejected - both modes already exist and are measured (FRUITJAM-61/62), so this is convenience, not capability. Recording the analysis so it is not re-derived. KEYBOARD side is easy: F12 is already handled at the top of hid_keyboard_apply() before the key-matrix diff, and F11 would sit alongside it. TWO REAL COSTS. (1) The framebuffers cannot coexist: 320x240 RGB565 is 153,600 bytes and 640x192 RGB565 is 245,760, which with the 230,988 base comes to 630,348 against 524,288 of SRAM. The only fit is a UNION - one 245,760-byte buffer reinterpreted as [240][320] or [192][640], since only one is live at a time - which puts RAM at ~91.4% PERMANENTLY, in both modes, dropping free heap+stack from ~139 KB to ~45 KB. That means paying the cropped path's memory cost even while running the 2x default the user chose to keep, and SD/USB under the reduced heap is still unverified. (2) The two modes need different DMA widths (2x uses 16-bit bus-replication, 2.5x uses 32-bit distinct pixels), so toggling means flipping native_pixel_mode at runtime - which is unsafe today, see FRUITJAM-65. ALSO NEEDED on toggle: swap the row LUT (active_line>>1 vs line*2/5), repaint the border columns/rows, and re-blit. REVISIT TRIGGER: someone actually wants to switch without reflashing, or RAM pressure eases. DO FRUITJAM-65 FIRST regardless - it is a latent bug on its own. COMPLETION CONDITION: F11 switches zoom on hardware with no desync and no visual latch across repeated toggles.

summary: Toggling native_pixel_mode off at runtime can leave the scanout DMA stuck at 16-bit
description: Latent bug in vendored lib/pico_hdmi/src/video_output.c, found while scoping FRUITJAM-64. NOT triggered today - video_output_set_native_pixel_mode() is called once in setup() and never changed - but it is a trap for any future runtime mode switch, and the symptom is identical to the fault this project spent a day chasing. MECHANISM: the scanout ISR writes the DMA control word only under a native-mode guard (video_output.c:627): if (native_pixel_mode) ch->al1_ctrl = posting_active_data ? dma_ctrl16[ch] : dma_ctrl32[ch]. So in native mode the channel ALTERNATES between 16- and 32-bit every line. hstx_resync() restores dma_ctrl32 under the SAME guard. Set native_pixel_mode=false while the channel happens to be in its 16-bit state and nothing ever restores 32-bit: the ISR stops writing al1_ctrl, and a resync will not fix it either because its restore is also guarded. The command stream then goes out at half width, the HSTX expander misreads everything after it, the FIFO stops back-pressuring and the link free-runs at ~2.67x - 160 fps at 60p, the same signature as FRUITJAM-49. It is a RACE on when the toggle lands: during a blanking line it is harmless, during active data it latches. Intermittent and boot-to-boot, which is exactly the class of fault this repo has repeatedly been burned by. FIX: restore dma_ctrl32 UNCONDITIONALLY in hstx_resync() rather than under the native_pixel_mode guard - the resync already reprograms the channels from frame start, so there is no case where leaving stale 16-bit ctrl is correct - and have any runtime toggle force a resync afterwards. This would be the SECOND local modification to this vendored library; record it in PROVENANCE.md alongside the RP2350-E5 fix, and report both upstream together. COMPLETION CONDITION: native_pixel_mode can be flipped repeatedly at runtime, under load, with no desync and no latch.

summary: Picker: halt the 6809 while the overlay is open; remap buttons to 3=UP 2=MOUNT+RESET 1=DOWN
description: Two changes to the FRUITJAM-50/51 disk picker, requested together. (1) HALT. The overlay previously froze only the DISPLAY - coco_machine_run_cycles() kept running, so the emulated machine carried on behind the menu. Now run_cycles() and render_frame() are skipped while g_pick_open. Two reasons: swapping a floppy under a STOPPED DOS is safer than under a running one, and it hands ~13 ms/field of core 0 back exactly while the overlay is on screen, which is when the user is looking at it and would most notice a desync (core-0 headroom tracks desync rate, FRUITJAM-58). Audio needed no special handling, which was the one real risk: audio_feed() already tops the I2S ring up with g_audio_last on underrun, and a held constant sample is DC - silence, not a sustained tone - so a halted machine is simply quiet. The real-time divide in the report is now guarded, because run_us_acc can legitimately be ~0 for a whole report period if the overlay was open throughout. VERIFIABLE with the FRUITJAM-60 probe: while the overlay is up, [cpu] PC should FREEZE and irq/s should read 0; both resume on close. (2) BUTTON REMAP, was 1=select 2=prev 3=next, now 3=UP/PREV, 2=MOUNT+RESET, 1=DOWN/NEXT - select in the middle of the physical row where it belongs, leaving the outer two as the up/down pair. Any button still opens the overlay when it is closed. Button 2 now also calls coco_machine_release_all_keys() then coco_machine_reset(), so the machine boots from the disk just selected. KNOWN ASYMMETRY, deliberate but worth revisiting: keyboard ENTER still does a live floppy swap with NO reset, the original FRUITJAM-50 behaviour ('mount is a floppy swap, not a reset'). Buttons and keys were previously equivalent and now are not. Left as specified rather than silently reversing a recorded decision for the keyboard path. ALSO STILL OPEN: there is no button equivalent of F12/cancel - button 2 always commits, so a button-only user cannot dismiss the picker without mounting something. A long-press on 2, or 1+3 together, would both work. On-screen hint updated to 'UP=3 DN=1 MOUNT+RST=2 F12=ESC' (29 of 32 columns). COMPLETION CONDITION: on hardware, the buttons move and mount as mapped, and the [cpu] probe shows PC frozen with irq/s=0 while the overlay is open. VERIFIED ON HARDWARE 2026-08-26 (docs/logs/fj66-picker2.log). Halt: avg run 13109 -> 590 us/field, 95.5% of core 0 handed back - better than the ~13 ms estimated; irq/s 60 -> 0; PC frozen at $A7D5; VDG hash static; FRUITJAM-60's '! SCREEN STATIC' raised after 5 s exactly as designed, and only during the halt. Buttons: '[btn] 3 open=0' opened the overlay, button 1 moved the selection 0 -> 1 (confirmed by the sel value printed at the next press - note the [btn] line prints sel BEFORE the move is applied, since the printf sits at the top of picker_task), button 2 mounted and warm-reset, and the machine returned to 1.26x with irq/s=60 and the blit back at 3171 us. The reset takes the warm path - PC never passes through $A089, BASIC's RAM-clear address seen at cold boot - which is correct for coco_machine_reset(). Also fixed two logging bugs the first test exposed: [btn] labelled the action's OLD button so pressing 3 logged '2', and a halted emulator reported '28.39x real-time' which reads as speed when nothing is running (now 'HALTED,'). SD confirmed working incidentally: 21 disks enumerated, full boot chain ok on the 73.4% default build. CLOSING. Remainder filed as FRUITJAM-67.

summary: Picker: button 2 cold-boots where keyboard ENTER swaps live — unify or document
description: Two loose ends left by FRUITJAM-66, both known and deliberate at the time, neither urgent. (1) NO BUTTON CANCEL. F12 dismisses the overlay without mounting, but there is no button equivalent - button 2 always commits - so a user with no keyboard attached cannot back out of the picker without swapping a disk and warm-resetting the machine. That is a real dead end on a button-only setup, and the reset makes it costly rather than merely annoying. Options: a long-press on button 2, or buttons 1+3 together (both outer buttons, easy to reach, no conflict with the existing single-press actions). btn_fell() only reports edges, so a long-press needs a held-duration check. (2) BUTTON/KEYBOARD DIVERGENCE. Button 2 mounts AND warm-resets so the machine boots from the selected disk; keyboard ENTER still does a live floppy swap with no reset, which is the original FRUITJAM-50 behaviour recorded as 'mount is a floppy swap, not a reset'. FRUITJAM-50/51 explicitly designed buttons and keys to be equivalent ('either input works at any time'); they no longer are. This was left as specified rather than silently reversing a recorded decision on the keyboard path, but the same action behaving differently by input method is a UX trap. THREE WAYS OUT, pick one: make ENTER also reset (unify on the new behaviour, reverses FRUITJAM-50's decision - do it knowingly); make button 2 not reset (unify on the old, but the user asked for the reset); or keep both and add a second binding for the other semantic, e.g. SHIFT+ENTER for mount-and-reset and a modified button press for swap-only. COMPLETION CONDITION: a button-only user can dismiss the picker without mounting, and mount semantics are either unified or deliberately documented as differing, on screen as well as in code. SUPERSEDED IN PART 2026-08-26: the no-button-cancel half is fixed by FRUITJAM-70 (a [CANCEL] row in the list). What REMAINS open here is only the second half - button 2 mounts and cold-boots where keyboard ENTER does a live floppy swap with no reset, so the two inputs still diverge. That divergence is now arguably CORRECT rather than accidental: buttons are the no-keyboard path, where a live swap is useless because there is no way to type DOS or RUN, while a keyboard user can swap under a running DOS on purpose. Decide whether to document it as intended or unify.

summary: ESC cancels the picker without leaking BREAK into the emulator
description: ESC now closes the overlay without mounting, which also unhalts the 6809 since the FRUITJAM-66 halt is gated purely on g_pick_open. CANCEL-ONLY, deliberately not a toggle like F12: HID 0x29 maps to DSCAN_BREAK, the CoCo BREAK key, so if ESC also OPENED the picker then BREAK would be unreachable whenever the overlay is closed - which is nearly always. THE SUBTLE PART, and it was a real leak rather than a theoretical one: while the overlay is open the picker block returns early, so g_prev_codes is never updated, and the open path had zeroed it. Closing and returning would leave the NEXT HID report seeing a still-held ESC as newly pressed and fire BREAK straight into BASIC the instant the user cancelled - stopping any running program. F12 never had this problem because it is unmapped (g_hid_to_dscan[0x45] == 0xFF) and harmless to let fall through. Fixed by copying the live codes into g_prev_codes on close, so the held ESC reads as already-down and generates no press; the eventual release then targets a key that was never pressed, which the matrix ignores. COMPLETION CONDITION: with a program running (10 GOTO 10 / RUN), open the picker, press ESC, and confirm the program is STILL RUNNING afterwards - i.e. no BREAK was delivered. VERIFIED ON HARDWARE 2026-08-26: ESC cancels the picker and no BREAK reaches BASIC. Closing.

summary: Button 2 does a full cold restart with the selected disk, not a warm reset
description: Requested because a warm reset was not a real restart. coco_machine_reset() is an authentic WARM reset - it re-asserts RESET and leaves RAM intact by design - so Color BASIC warm-started with the previous program and variables still in place: no banner, no RAM clear. Confirmed on hardware before the change, where PC never passed through $A089, BASIC's cold-boot RAM-clear address. ADDED coco_machine_cold_reset(): wipe g_ram[65536], then re-assert RESET. It works because Color BASIC decides warm vs cold by testing a warm-start flag held in low RAM - with RAM zeroed the flag cannot match, so the ROM takes the COLD path, which is what a power cycle looks like. RAM ONLY: the cartridge ROM and the mounted .dsk live outside g_ram and must survive, or the machine would cold-boot with no disk in the drive, defeating the point. SAM/PIA/VDG are left alone for the same reason the warm path does - BASIC re-initialises them as it boots. Mount happens BEFORE the reset so the disk is already in drive 0 when the ROM comes up. Hint updated to 'UP=3 DN=1 MNT+BOOT=2 ESC=CANCEL'. COMPLETION CONDITION: on hardware, button 2 on a disk produces the cold-boot banner and PC passing through $A089 in the [cpu] probe, with the selected disk readable afterwards. BUG FOUND AND FIXED 2026-08-26, reported from hardware as 'cold boot is unpredictable, but kinda works probably' - and unpredictable was the precise symptom. The first version wiped RAM but left the SAM alone, on the same reasoning the warm path uses (BASIC re-initialises SAM/PIA/VDG as it boots). That reasoning does NOT hold once RAM is wiped. If the previous program left the SAM in all-RAM mode - TY set by a write to $FFDF - the read decode at coco_mem_cycle sends $A000-$BFFF to g_ram instead of rom_read(), and g_ram had just been zeroed, so the BASIC ROM reads as zeros. The reset VECTOR still works because $FFE0+ bypasses the TY test, so the CPU jumps to the correct address and then executes zeros; and it can never recover, because the instruction that would clear TY lives in the ROM it can no longer read. Whether a cold boot worked therefore depended entirely on what the last program had done to the SAM - hence intermittent. FIX: call g_m.sam->reset() and clear the port's own sam_ty/sam_f shadows before resetting the CPU. This is correct emulation rather than a workaround: on real hardware the SAM's RESET input clears these. sam_f matters too - a stale display base would leave the VDG scanning from the wrong address. PIAs are deliberately still NOT reset: unlike the SAM they do not gate ROM visibility, so the ROM can execute and programs them during init, and mc6821_reset() would clobber the in_source/in_sink levels and delegate hookups that machine init installs AFTER its own reset call. LESSON: 'BASIC re-initialises it on boot' is only valid for state that does not gate the ROM's own readability. VERIFIED ON HARDWARE 2026-08-26 after the SAM fix: cold boot now behaves predictably. Closing.

summary: [CANCEL] row in the picker list, so buttons alone can back out
description: Buttons are the NO-KEYBOARD path - that is the whole reason they exist - so every action must be reachable from the three buttons alone. Cancel was not. ESC (FRUITJAM-68) and F12 both need a keyboard, and button 2 always commits, which since FRUITJAM-69 also means a COLD BOOT. So opening the picker by accident with no keyboard attached left NO way out except mounting something and rebooting the machine - a dead end in exactly the case buttons are for. The same bug made an empty /COCO/DSK an unescapable empty box. REJECTED: a long-press on button 2, or a 1+3 chord. Both work mechanically but neither is DISCOVERABLE, and discoverability matters most precisely on the device with no keyboard to tell you otherwise. CHOSEN: a trailing [CANCEL] row in the list. No new gesture, documents itself on screen, and sits one press from the top because the selection wraps - UP from the first disk lands on it. The list is now PICK_COUNT = g_dsk_count + 1 entries with PICK_IS_CANCEL(i) as the test; both the button and keyboard movement paths use it, so ENTER on [CANCEL] behaves the same as ESC. The 'NO .DSK FILES' message moved below the list, since row 2 is now the [CANCEL] entry. COMPLETION CONDITION: with no keyboard attached, open the picker and return to the emulator without mounting a disk or rebooting. VERIFIED ON HARDWARE 2026-08-26: button-only escape works - the picker can be opened and left with no keyboard, no mount and no reboot. Closing.

summary: Picker remembers the last mounted disk across reboots
description: Requested after the same behaviour in the AMOLED port: selecting a disk should survive a power cycle, so the device comes back with the disk you were using rather than resetting to AUTO.DSK. Matters most on the no-keyboard path, where re-selecting means navigating the picker every single boot. STORED AS A FILENAME, NOT AN INDEX, in 0:/coco/lastdsk.txt - indices shift the moment a .dsk is added to or removed from the card, which would silently mount the WRONG image, and a name fails safe instead. Plain text and hand-editable; deleting it falls back to AUTO.DSK. Lives in /coco/ not /coco/dsk/ so scan_dsk_dir() can never enumerate it, and is named .txt so it cannot be mistaken for a disk image. BOOT PRECEDENCE: remembered disk, then AUTO.DSK, then coco.dsk. The user's most recent explicit choice outranks the static AUTO.DSK marker. A remembered disk that has since been removed from the card logs '[last disk X not on card]' and falls through to AUTO.DSK rather than failing to boot. RESTRUCTURED the boot block so scan_dsk_dir() runs FIRST - resolving a remembered name back to an index needs the list to exist - and boot then reuses mount_dsk_index() instead of duplicating the load/mount path. That function gained a remember flag: the picker's two commit sites pass true, boot passes false, because restoring a disk is not the user choosing it and would rewrite the marker identically on every boot, costing an SD write and card wear for nothing. g_pick_sel now opens on whatever is actually mounted, so the highlight and the drive agree the first time the picker is opened. A read-only or full card is not fatal - persistence is simply skipped, with a log line. ALSO ADDED: the boot line now says WHY a disk was chosen, '(remembered)' vs '(AUTO.DSK)', because the two were previously indistinguishable in the log - which cost time during this very change. VERIFIED ON HARDWARE 2026-08-26: mounted tiny.dsk via the picker, rebooted, and boot reported '[disk mounted: tiny.dsk (remembered) -> DIR/LOAD]'.

summary: PMODE 4 NTSC artifact colour, with F11 cycling the phase
description: PMODE 4 is VDG mode RG6 (gm==7): 256x192, 1 bit per pixel. On a real NTSC CoCo the pixel rate (~7.16 MHz) is exactly TWICE the colour subcarrier (3.579545 MHz), so alternating pixel patterns land on the subcarrier and the TV's colour decoder reads them as chroma - one-bit data shows as four colours keyed on PIXEL PAIRS: 00 black, 01 and 10 the two artifact colours, 11 foreground. Effective horizontal resolution halves to 128; that is authentic, not a bug, and is why artifact games look chunky. Software that depends on it (Donkey King, Pitfall II) is near-unreadable in plain mono, which is what this port did before. NOTHING TO SWITCH ON: the vendored xroar_core contains ZERO artifact/cross-colour code - XRoar implements it in its video/NTSC modules, which were never part of the minimal extraction (only mc6847.c and the fonts came across). Unlike FRUITJAM-42's font work this could NOT be enabled by lifting a library.json exclusion; it had to be written. Implemented as a pair lookup rather than an NTSC simulation, which is what the other RP2350 ports do and is sufficient for the software that needs it. CHEAP because two things lined up: palette slots 10-15 were spare in the 16-entry palette so the artifact colours disturb no existing mapping, and the renderer already emits 4bpp palette indices, making it one table lookup per pixel pair.
