F11 CYCLES off -> phase A -> phase B -> off. Three states rather than a plain toggle for two reasons: without OFF there is no way back to plain mono, and BOTH phases are needed because which one a given game expects is arbitrary - that is exactly what 'press reset until the colours look right' means in CoCo manuals. Handled before the picker's modal check so it works whether or not the overlay is open; F11 is unmapped in g_hid_to_dscan so it cannot leak into BASIC. Default OFF, so existing behaviour is unchanged until asked for - flipping that default is a one-liner if artifact-on proves the better default. ALSO FIXED: render_rg6_frame() ignored css entirely and always drew white, which was wrong for CSS=0 (green on black) independently of artifacting. NOT DONE: the phase is not persisted across reboots (cf. FRUITJAM-71 for the disk), and the artifact RGB values are eyeballed approximations of CoCo blue/orange rather than measured. COMPLETION CONDITION: an artifact-dependent PMODE 4 program renders in colour on hardware, and F11 reaches both phases plus off. VERIFIED ON HARDWARE 2026-08-26: PMODE 4 artifact colour renders and F11 cycles the phases. Closing. Remainder filed as FRUITJAM-74.

summary: Artifact polish: persist the phase, and calibrate the artifact RGB values
description: The 20% left over from FRUITJAM-73, filed rather than holding that issue open. (1) PHASE IS NOT PERSISTED. It resets to OFF on every boot, so a user who needs phase B for their game re-presses F11 twice after each power cycle - the same annoyance FRUITJAM-71 fixed for disk selection, and it matters most on the no-keyboard button path where F11 is not even reachable. Note that gap: artifact phase currently has NO button binding at all, so a button-only user cannot turn artifacts on. Persisting it would at least let the setting be chosen once with a keyboard and then stick. Reuse the FRUITJAM-71 mechanism (a small file on SD); consider one settings file rather than a second bare marker. (2) THE ARTIFACT RGB VALUES ARE EYEBALLED, not measured: g_pal[10] is 0x30/0x50/0xE0 and g_pal[11] is 0xE0/0x60/0x18, chosen to look like CoCo blue and orange rather than derived from NTSC decoding of the actual pattern or compared against real hardware. They are two constants and easy to change. Worth comparing against the waveshare pizero port and the other XRoar RP2350 ports, which the user reports already implement this. COMPLETION CONDITION: the artifact setting survives a reboot, and the colours have been compared side by side against another port or real hardware and either adjusted or confirmed.

summary: HSTX desync rate is driven by core-0 CODE LAYOUT in flash, not by how much work it does
description: THE SIGNIFICANT FINDING of 2026-08-26, and it reframes FRUITJAM-58, -53 and -38. Chasing an 80x desync regression produced a four-point bisect on one board, adjacent in time: A = FRUITJAM-71 only, 7.6 min, 0 desyncs (0/hr), avg run 13156 us. B = +FRUITJAM-72 live, 8.8 min, 170 (1166/hr), avg run 14600. C = +FRUITJAM-72 with the whole block behind a volatile false so every byte stays in the image at the same addresses but NEVER EXECUTES, 8.7 min, 140 (964/hr), avg run 14643. D = the full build with blit_frame() moved to .time_critical RAM, 23.1 min, 12 (31/hr), avg run 13068. C IS THE RESULT: ~110 lines of code that never runs cost +1.5 ms/field and took desyncs from 0 to 964/hr. The cost is the code's PRESENCE, not its execution. MECHANISM: core 0's per-field path - loop(), blit_frame(), audio_feed(), picker_task() - executes from FLASH via the XIP cache. Only the two core-1 scanline callbacks carried RAM_FUNC; HOT_FUNC already put the 6809 core and the machine layer in .time_critical, but the host-side path was never given the same treatment. Any edit that shifts those addresses reshuffles cache-line mapping, and flash-fetch stalls starve the HSTX FIFO. The project already knew the principle - g_pal is forced into RAM with a comment saying an XIP stall there starves the FIFO - it was just never applied to core 0's own hot loop. Note blit itself barely moved (2904 -> 2998 us): the 1.5 ms was blit_frame THRASHING the XIP cache against the rest of core 0's flash-resident code, not the blit being slow. FIX APPLIED: RAM_FUNC on blit_frame(), the largest flash-resident chunk of the per-field path at ~3 ms. CONSEQUENCES FOR PAST WORK, all of which must now be re-read: (1) FRUITJAM-53's NeoPixel bisect showing 0/0/0/15 across builds never had a plausible mechanism - layout is one. (2) 'Desync rate tracks core-0 headroom' (proposed earlier the same day from 13.0 ms -> 15/hr vs 16.0 ms -> 25/hr) is CONFOUNDED: avg run itself moves with layout, as C proves. (3) Same-day scatter that looked like noise - fj61-crop 0/hr against fj62-edge 431/hr - is consistent with layout. (4) Any future A/B of a code change is invalid unless the hot path is layout-immune, because the act of adding code is itself a variable. COMPLETION CONDITION: this is the write-up; the remaining work is FRUITJAM-76 (move the rest of the per-field path to RAM and confirm over a multi-hour run). CONFIRMED OVER A LONG RUN 2026-08-27: 3.3 hours, 3850 reports, 0 reboots, 69 desyncs = 21/hr against 964/hr for the same code before the fix. A 46x reduction, and the rate is back in the historical healthy band (11-15/hr).

summary: Move the rest of core 0's per-field path into RAM and confirm over a long run
description: Follow-up to FRUITJAM-75, which moved blit_frame() to .time_critical and took desyncs from 964/hr to 31/hr. 31/hr is normal-baseline territory (today's healthy builds measured 11-15/hr) but it is not zero, and build A measured 0 in 7.6 min. Still FLASH-RESIDENT and running every field on core 0: loop() itself, audio_feed(), picker_task(), basic_at_prompt(), autotype_task() and the once-per-second report block. Each is a candidate. DO IT ONE AT A TIME AND MEASURE - the whole point of FRUITJAM-75 is that adding or moving code is itself a variable, so a batch change tells you nothing about which part mattered. Watch the RAM budget: .time_critical comes out of SRAM, currently 73.4% used, and FRUITJAM-61's cropped scaling path would need 91.4% if it is ever enabled. ALSO WORTH TRYING: raising the XIP cache's effectiveness rather than evicting code from flash - check whether the partition/linker layout can keep the hot path cache-aligned, which would be cheaper in SRAM. COMPLETION CONDITION: a multi-hour capture at a rate that no longer moves when unrelated code is added - i.e. add 100 lines of dead code and see the rate NOT change. That negative test is the real proof, not a low number on one build. DONE 2026-08-27, negative test PASSED. Moved the whole per-field path to .time_critical RAM: loop(), blit_frame(), audio_feed(), picker_task(), btn_fell(), basic_at_prompt(), autotype_task(), dscan_for(). Cost +4152 bytes of SRAM, 73.4% -> 74.2%. MEASUREMENTS, both idle-confirmed (zero non-ROM PCs sampled, so no program was running to confound the load): E2 baseline 13.8 min, 3 desyncs (13.0/hr), avg run 12583 us, blit 2588 us. F, the same build plus 96 lines of FLASH-RESIDENT, referenced, never-executed ballast behind a volatile false - deliberately the same shape as the FRUITJAM-72 block that cost 964/hr - 13.7 min, 1 desync (4.4/hr), avg run 12621 us, blit 2640 us. AVG RUN AGREED TO 38 us, 0.3%, against the +1500 us (12%) that the identical kind of change caused before the fix. That is the real evidence; the desync counts (3 vs 1) are single-digit Poisson noise and are NOT claimed as an improvement. The hot path is layout-immune. SIDE BENEFIT: moving the rest of the path out of flash also made it faster - avg run 13049 -> 12583 us and blit 2999 -> 2588 us versus FRUITJAM-75's blit-only build, roughly 465 us/field of headroom recovered, which matters because core 0 is the constrained core. STILL IN FLASH BY NECESSITY: USBHost.task() (TinyUSB) and the Serial.printf report block. The report runs once a second so it evicts cache lines rarely, and the negative test passing with both still in flash says they are not currently a problem - but they are the first suspects if layout sensitivity ever returns. CONSEQUENCE: A/B measurement in this repo is now valid. FRUITJAM-58's onset hunt and FRUITJAM-53's NeoPixel claim can both be attacked properly, which they could not be before - the act of adding instrumentation was changing the thing being measured.

summary: Auto-run the first program on a button-mounted disk
description: After button 2 mounts a disk and cold-boots, read the RSDOS directory (track 17, sectors 3-11), find the first runnable entry and type the command at the DECB prompt: file type 0 -> RUN"NAME", type 2 -> LOADM"NAME":EXEC. Types 1 and 3 are skipped so a data file first on the disk cannot win. Buttons only - the no-keyboard path. Trigger waits for the screen to CLEAR then for a SETTLED OK (45 fields stable + 60 settle): the first attempt fired 1.18 s after the button and lost leading characters, because DECB prints its banner and OK before it polls the key matrix. Autotype holds each key 3 fields, gaps 2; " is SHIFT+2. VERIFIED ON HARDWARE 2026-08-27.

summary: Restore boot-progress NeoPixels by default; record the measured cost of a lit strip
description: FRUITJAM-53 gated the boot LEDs off on evidence that does not survive re-measurement, and the user noticed the loss directly - 'it used to flash red at startup before we started debugging these issues'. COCO_NEOPIXEL defaults to 1 again: boot progress across the strip, which is then LEFT LIT. WS2812s latch, so the last colour persists with no state machine held and nothing touching the strip at runtime. MEASURED COST, recorded at the flag so it is a deliberate choice: ~21/hr desyncs with the strip lit against ~5.9/hr dark, about 3.5x. It tracks illumination, not code - see FRUITJAM-53 for the three-arm measurement. User accepted the trade. NOTE A REAL GAP LEFT OPEN: there is still NO way to turn the strip off. WS2812s hold their last colour until power is removed, and neither COCO_NEOPIXEL=0 nor a reset clears them - a =0 build simply inherits whatever the previous firmware left, across reflashes. An unconditional clear-at-boot was written and then removed at the user's request, since they want it lit. If a dark strip is ever wanted, that clear is the mechanism and it needs a power cycle otherwise. ALSO NOT DONE: a same-session LEDs-dark control. The dark figure quoted is the overnight run; the two lit arms are same-morning and agree. If the ~3.5x ever matters enough to revisit, that control is the first thing to run.

summary: Multi-drive support: assign .dsk images to drives 1-3, not just drive 0
description: The picker currently manages ONE disk - whatever is mounted as drive 0 - and coco_machine_mount_dsk() takes a single image. Real Disk BASIC addresses four drives, and plenty of software expects a program disk in 0 and data in 1. Fine for demonstration as-is; needed before anyone uses this as a working machine. SCOPE: extend the machine layer to hold up to four images with per-drive write-protect (g_dsk_wp is already per-machine, not per-drive), have the FDC's drive select in DSKREG choose between them, and extend the overlay so a disk can be assigned to a drive rather than just mounted. UI QUESTION worth settling first: the current picker is a flat list where selecting means 'mount to drive 0'. Four drives needs either a drive column in the list, or a two-step select-disk-then-select-drive, or four separate lists. The button path (no keyboard) constrains this - three buttons and a wrapping list is all that is guaranteed available, so whatever is chosen has to be reachable that way. NOTE the interaction with FRUITJAM-71: only drive 0's selection is persisted; multi-drive means persisting an assignment set, which is the point at which lastdsk.txt should probably become a small settings file. COMPLETION CONDITION: a .dsk can be assigned to drive 1 and read from BASIC with DRIVE 1, and the assignment survives a reboot.

summary: Cache SD images in flash so disk switching is a memcpy, not a 160 ms SD read
description: mount_dsk_index() blocks core 0 for the length of a ~160 KB SD read on every disk swap. Caching the card's contents in on-board flash would make switching near-instant and remove SD from the runtime path entirely. CAPACITY IS NOT THE PROBLEM: flash is 16,773,120 bytes with 255,516 used by firmware, so ~15.7 MB free. 21 standard 35-track single-sided images at 161,280 bytes each is 3.23 MB, plus ~24 KB of ROMs - it fits roughly four times over, and even 40-track double-sided images (368,640 each) would only reach ~7.7 MB. Caveat: only one image is CONFIRMED at 161,280 (from the boot log); the rest are assumed standard. TWO REAL CONSTRAINTS. (1) Writing flash at runtime requires that NEITHER core is executing from XIP during the erase/program, or the fetch stalls. FRUITJAM-76 already moved core 0's whole per-field path into .time_critical RAM, so core 0 is most of the way there; core 1's DMA-IRQ handler would need the same treatment, and it is the more sensitive of the two because starving the HSTX FIFO is what desyncs the link. (2) Disk WRITES must not go to flash - 4 KB sector erase per sector write, plus wear. SHAPE: flash as a read-only image store, PSRAM as the mutable working copy (PSRAM is volatile - DRAM with a refresh controller - so it cannot be the store), SD as the source of truth to sync from and back to. Switching disks then becomes a memcpy from XIP into PSRAM. OPEN QUESTION: whether to mount read-only images directly from memory-mapped XIP and only copy to PSRAM when a write occurs, which would make switching free but puts FDC reads on the XIP path. COMPLETION CONDITION: images load from flash at boot with no SD access, and a disk swap completes without a measurable core-0 stall.

summary: F10 toggles the NeoPixel strip on/off after boot
description: The boot-progress strip is left lit deliberately (FRUITJAM-77) - the red/green/blue palette echoes the original CoCo badge and the case's integrated light-well diffuses it nicely. But there is currently NO way to turn it off short of a power cycle, because WS2812s latch their last colour and nothing drives the strip at runtime. F10 should toggle it. CHEAP: the strip is static, so a toggle is create/clear/show or create/restore/show and then free the state machine again - no per-field cost, nothing held. Remember the measured trade so the toggle is meaningful: desync rate is ~21/hr lit against ~5.9/hr dark, so this doubles as a stability control, not just an aesthetic one. KEY MAP CONTEXT: F12 is the picker, F11 cycles artifact phase, F10 would be this. F1 and F2 must stay RESERVED - the CoCo 3 has its own F1/F2 (DSCAN_F1/F2 already exist in the core), so they belong to the emulated machine if GIME ever lands. NOT COVERED: the rainbow idle cycle is a separate thing, still blocked by FRUITJAM-47 (show() bit-bangs with interrupts off for ~450 us on core 0 and desyncs video; needs a DMA-fed WS2812 writer). This issue is on/off of the static strip only. NO BUTTON BINDING is proposed - the three buttons are spoken for by the picker, so on a keyboard-less setup the strip stays as it booted. COMPLETION CONDITION: F10 extinguishes and restores the strip on hardware.

summary: Sector-granular write-back of disk images to SD, so SAVE actually persists
description: Today the FDC writes sectors into the mutable PSRAM image (g_dsk) and nothing ever writes them back - SAVE works, DIR shows the file, and a reboot or a disk swap loses it. Nothing calls f_write on a .dsk. For a machine meant to be USED rather than demonstrated this is the biggest functional hole. MECHANISM, sector-granular by preference: the FDC already knows the byte offset of the sector it just wrote, so f_lseek to hdr + lsn*256 and write 256 bytes. No 160 KB rewrite, no read-modify-write of the whole image. Track dirty sectors so a flush is bounded, and flush on swap and eject as a backstop. Whole-image rewrite is explicitly REJECTED: it makes every save cost a 160 ms card write and scales with image size rather than with what changed. LATENCY BUDGET, and this is the useful insight: real CoCo software already parks its UI in a 'just one moment' state while the drive spins and chatters, so existing software TOLERATES disk latency by design. That tolerance is headroom - but it should be spent on RELIABILITY, not inherited as drama. The goal is saves that are faster and less theatrical than the original while being just as trustworthy. DESIGN PRINCIPLE FOR THE OVERLAY, recorded because it is what distinguishes this port and should not be lost: the overlay speaks the MACHINE'S visual language - VDG font, 32x16 cell grid, machine palette, anchored to the 6847 active area. It reads as part of the computer rather than as a host-side configuration tool bolted on top. Two counter-examples the user named explicitly: FujiNet's separate application for picking images and then matching them to drive numbers (disliked - it is a mode change into a different machine), and the ESP32 CoCo's overlay (not terrible, but not CoCo-like). REJECTED DIRECTION, so it is not relitigated: do NOT build a separate configuration application, and do not make drive assignment a mode the user enters and leaves. The illusion to protect is inserting a disk and getting a disk - fluid, in-idiom, no ceremony. This constrains FRUITJAM-78's multi-drive UI directly. COMPLETION CONDITION: SAVE from BASIC, power-cycle, and LOAD the file back; and a save costs a bounded write proportional to sectors changed rather than to image size. VERIFIED ON HARDWARE 2026-08-28: SAVE from BASIC persists across a power cycle and LOAD brings it back. IMPLEMENTED: the FDC reports each written sector's byte OFFSET via coco_machine_set_dsk_write_callback() - no data is copied, since it is already in the PSRAM image the host owns - and flush_dsk_writes() drains at most 4 sectors per field from loop(), never from inside the emulation call. Offsets are deduplicated, so a program rewriting one sector in a loop costs one card write. Queue overflow (>16 pending) degrades to a full-image rewrite rather than persisting a partially-updated disk. A disk swap flushes first, so switching cannot strand unwritten sectors. f_open per flush rather than a held FIL: a held handle would have to survive swaps, SD removal and the picker, and FatFs gives no cheap way to validate one; saves are rare enough that the directory lookup is affordable. Closing. Remainder filed as FRUITJAM-87. NOTE: shipped but GATED OFF by default under COCO_DSK_WRITEBACK pending FRUITJAM-88 - the mechanism is verified, the disk image it persists is not.

summary: CYCLES_PER_FRAME and FRAME_US are derived from 60 Hz, not NTSC's 59.94 Hz
description: coco_main.cpp:231 comments 'Authentic NTSC CoCo: ~0.895 MHz / 60 Hz = 14915 6809 cycles per field'. The divisor is wrong: NTSC field rate is 59.94 Hz, not 60. Correct figures: CPU clock is 14.31818 MHz / 16 = 894,886 Hz; field rate is 15734.264 / 262.5 = 59.94 Hz; so cycles per field is 894886 / 59.94 = 14,930 and the field period is 16,683 us. We use 14,915 and 16,762. XRoar's own VDG_FRAME_DURATION is 262 lines, consistent with the corrected numbers. NET EFFECT: we run the 6809 at 14915 * (1e6/16762) = 889,750 Hz against 894,886 - about 0.57% SLOW. Audio pitch is off by ~10 cents (inaudible) and timing loops run marginally long. WHAT IT IS NOT: this does not affect the emulated machine's INTERNAL consistency. The field-sync IRQ is generated by the VDG's event queue from cycle counts, not from CYCLES_PER_FRAME - which is why the [cpu] probe reads a steady irq/s=60. CYCLES_PER_FRAME only sets how much emulation runs per call and how we pace to wall clock. So the error is in the wall-clock relationship, not in the machine's own timebase. Recorded because it was raised as a candidate cause for a demo crashing after several minutes and should NOT be treated as one: software that breaks on a 0.57% clock error would break on real hardware variation too. Fix it for correctness, not as a bug hunt. NOTE the audio resampler takes both values (coco_machine_audio_init(CYCLES_PER_FRAME, FRAME_US)) and derives cycles-per-48kHz-sample from their ratio, so changing one without the other would detune the I2S feed - change both together and re-check that the ring neither starves nor overflows. COMPLETION CONDITION: both constants corrected with the derivation in the comment, and audio still clean on hardware.

summary: CoCo 3 (GIME) support: what it would actually take
description: Never attempted here - no prior issue existed. Recording the analysis so the decision is informed rather than aspirational. NOT A BARRIER: the emulation itself. XRoar implements GIME upstream; our extraction simply did not take it (lib/xroar_core/src has mc6809, mc6847, mc6883, mc6821 - no tcc1014). So it is an extraction-plus-glue job, not new emulation work. THE HARD BARRIER IS CPU THROUGHPUT. The CoCo 3 runs at 1.79 MHz in fast mode. We sit at ~1.33x real-time at 0.895 MHz, so doubling the cycles per field puts us at roughly 0.67x - we cannot keep up. That needs about 2x more emulation throughput, and the sibling AMOLED port's DWT profiling says where the 2x is NOT: a 6809 bus cycle costs ~266 host clocks at 250 MHz, of which coco_mem_cycle is ~23 (~9%) and mc6809_run is the other ~91%. Their note is explicit - 'this retires a line of work: AMOLED-32, -53 and -56 were all tuning that 9%'. We have ALREADY done the equivalent work here (SAM decode only on $FFC0-$FFDF writes, PIA IRQ behind pia_irq_dirty, HOT_FUNC residency, -O2 with -Os stripped, SUPPRESS_RENDER_SCANLINE), so the memory path is spent and capped at 9% regardless. The only lever with 2x in it is replacing or restructuring mc6809_run - a leaner 6809 core (Fayzullin's, RetroArch's compact, or threaded dispatch), or a hybrid clock model that runs free between HS/FS anchor points. Both cost accuracy; see coco-rp2350-43b's docs/performance.md for the original framing of that contingency. A SLOW-MODE-ONLY CoCo 3 (0.89 MHz) would run today and is a legitimate scope reduction - much CoCo 3 software never switches to fast mode. SECOND BARRIER, RAM: 512K does not fit. SRAM is 520K total with 389K already used. PSRAM has the capacity but routes every memory cycle through QMI instead of single-cycle SRAM, compounding the throughput problem. A 128K CoCo 3 is borderline at 128K + 389K = 517K of 520K. THIRD, VIDEO: GIME's 640-wide modes break the pixel-doubling design - but FRUITJAM-61 already built the 640-wide scanout path (640x192 RGB565, row-pointer LUT, native_pixel_mode off), so that groundwork exists. FOURTH, THE MMU: eight 8K banks means a lookup on every memory access, added to the hottest path we have. COMPLETION CONDITION: a decision recorded - slow-mode-only CoCo 3, full CoCo 3 behind a core swap, or not doing it - rather than an implementation.

summary: Move blit_frame (and possibly render) to core 1, which is nearly idle
description: Core 0 is the constrained core at ~1.33x real-time; core 1 does almost nothing. Its main loop is spin plus core1_background(), which in DVI mode is compose_service() early-returning and one flag check. The real work is the DMA IRQ at ~31.5 kHz, and in pointer mode that ISR is a single array load from g_row[] plus two register writes. Meanwhile blit_frame() costs 2,588 us of core 0's 16,683 us field. PRIOR ART: the sibling AMOLED port already did this (AMOLED-57, 'VDG render on core 1 -> real-time emulation, full screen'). Their core 1 runs render 913 us + blit 7,516 us = ~8.5 ms, about 51% of budget, and it is what took that port to real-time. Ours would be far cheaper because HSTX scans out directly instead of scaling and rotating to a panel. TWO REAL PROBLEMS. (1) There is ONE framebuffer and no double-buffering, so moving the blit moves the tear race rather than fixing it - core 1 would be writing the buffer it is also scanning out. Double buffering at 320x240 RGB565 costs another 153,600 bytes; RAM is at 74.2% so it fits, but not alongside FRUITJAM-61's cropped path. (2) Anything that stalls core 1 now stalls the scanline ISR, and starving the HSTX FIFO is precisely what desyncs the link (see docs/hstx-lessons.md). A blit that overruns its slot is a desync, not a dropped frame - the failure mode is worse than on the AMOLED port. SEQUENCING: FRUITJAM-63 (byte-at-a-time blit) should probably come first, since it makes whatever ends up on core 1 cheaper, and it is a contained change. COMPLETION CONDITION: blit runs on core 1, core-0 avg run drops by roughly the blit cost, and a multi-hour capture shows no increase in desync rate.

summary: Rain demo on tiny.dsk freezes on desktop XRoar too — not a port bug
description: Recorded so this is not re-investigated. SYMPTOM ON HARDWARE: the rain demo runs for minutes, then the screen stops updating while the emulator stays healthy - fields advancing, 59 fps, irq/s=60, no reboots. The FRUITJAM-60 probe caught the 6809 pinned at PC=$FF4A, inside the WD2797 FDC register window ($FF48-$FF4B). Code does not live there; the CPU had jumped into I/O space and was executing register reads as opcodes, almost certainly landing on a branch-to-self. DIFFERENTIAL TEST: the same image (~/Desktop/coco/dsk/tiny.dsk, 161,280 bytes, byte-identical to ~/github/tiny-agent/build/tiny.dsk) was run on desktop XRoar 1.10 via homebrew, machine 'cocous' (NTSC CoCo, original 6847, matching our COCO_VDG_T1=0). It ALSO froze, with the emulator process alive and healthy. CONCLUSION: the fault is not in this port's glue - not the memory map, not the FDC, not our timing or IRQ generation. WHAT IS NOT RULED OUT: both are XRoar 6809 cores (1.10 there, our 1.11 extraction), so a bug shared by both remains possible; and the two may have frozen at different points in the demo rather than identically. WRONG TURN WORTH RECORDING: PC landing in the FDC window was initially read as evidence the FDC caused it, on the theory that unimplemented WD2797 commands (Read Address / Read Track / Write Track, noted as unimplemented at coco_machine.cpp:513) had hung the driver. That does not follow - a wild jump has to land somewhere, and I/O space is a plausible resting place because register reads can decode as a self-branch. The landing site is not the cause. TO GO FURTHER, if anyone wants to: restart desktop XRoar with its GDB stub (xroar -m cocous -gdb -load-fd0 tiny.dsk), reproduce, and read the PC at the moment it dies - which the board can only sample once a second. CLOSED as not-our-bug by user decision; reopen only if the same freeze appears with software that runs correctly on real hardware.

summary: Write-back remainder: drive 0 only, untested overflow path, no write-protect control
description: The 20% left over from FRUITJAM-81, which is verified working for the normal case. (1) DRIVE 0 ONLY. g_dsk_path tracks the single mounted image, so write-back follows whatever the picker mounted. FRUITJAM-78's multi-drive work must extend this to a path per drive or writes will go to the wrong file - that is a data-loss bug waiting for multi-drive, so the two should land together. (2) THE OVERFLOW PATH IS UNTESTED. More than 16 pending sectors triggers a full-image rewrite (161,280 bytes). It is the safe fallback by design, but nothing has exercised it - a program writing many sectors quickly (a disk copy, a large binary save) would be the trigger. Worth forcing once to confirm it does not stall core 0 long enough to desync the link. (3) NO WRITE-PROTECT CONTROL. g_dsk_wp exists in the machine layer and is always false, so every mounted disk is writable. There is no way for a user to protect an image, and no indication in the picker that mounting something means it can be modified. (4) FLUSH COST IS UNMEASURED. The 4-sectors-per-field bound was chosen by reasoning, not measurement: during a disk operation the emulated CPU is halted waiting on the FDC, so the card write lands inside latency the software already expects. Nobody has checked what a flush actually costs in us/field or whether it moves the desync rate against the 7.6/hr baseline. (5) FORMAT IS STILL UNIMPLEMENTED - Write Track and friends remain stubbed (coco_machine.cpp), so a disk cannot be formatted in place, only written to. COMPLETION CONDITION: write-back is per-drive, the overflow path has been exercised on hardware, and the flush cost is measured. ADDITIONAL, found 2026-08-28: the '4 sectors per field' bound is NOT actually bounded. The log shows six flushes inside the same millisecond, because during a disk operation the emulated CPU is halted waiting on the FDC, so coco_machine_run_cycles() returns immediately and loop() spins far faster than once per field. The flush therefore drains as fast as the card allows rather than at the rate reasoned about. Not harmful in itself - the card write is still off the emulation call path - but the reasoning behind the constant was wrong and the real per-field cost is still unmeasured. CORRECTION 2026-08-28: the 16-slot overflow path is effectively UNREACHABLE, not merely untested. Measured on hardware, the pending queue never exceeded 2 sectors even for 8 KB+ SAVEM writes, because loop() spins while the CPU is halted on the FDC so the flush drains far faster than sectors accumulate. The queue was sized for a burst that does not happen. Either shrink it and drop the full-image fallback, or leave it as harmless insurance - but do not spend time testing a path nothing can reach.

summary: SAVEM corrupts the in-memory disk image — multi-sector FDC write path
description: DATA CORRUPTION. Found 2026-08-28 while testing FRUITJAM-81's write-back. After 'SAVEM"SCREEN",&H400,&H5FF,&H400' on tiny.dsk, a subsequent DIR returns garbage. NOT A WRITE-BACK BUG: DIR reads the directory from the IN-MEMORY PSRAM image through the FDC, not from the SD card, so the corruption is in the image itself. FRUITJAM-81 only added a callback AFTER the existing memcpy in fdc_finish() and changed nothing about which offset is written. This is a pre-existing fault in the FDC write path that SAVEM appears to be the first thing to exercise - single-sector writes from SAVE work correctly and persist, verified the same session. SUSPECT: multi-sector or multi-granule write sequences. Reads use the same dsk_offset(track, side, sector) and have always worked, so the geometry maths is probably sound; more likely the track/sector registers are not advanced correctly across a multi-sector write, so successive sectors land on top of each other or on the directory track. Worth checking how RSDOS issues the write - whether it re-issues a command per sector or relies on the controller stepping - against what the WD2797 emulation does in fdc_finish()/the command handler. CONSEQUENCE, and it is why this is high: write-back faithfully persists whatever is in the image, so a corrupted image is written to the SD card and the .dsk on the card is damaged. That happened here to tiny.dsk; clean copies survive at ~/Desktop/coco/dsk/tiny.dsk and ~/github/tiny-agent/build/tiny.dsk (byte-identical, 161,280 bytes). Until this is fixed, SAVEM on an image you care about will destroy it. NOTE the interaction: this was harmless before FRUITJAM-81 because corruption stayed in volatile PSRAM and a reboot restored the disk. Write-back made a latent bug permanent. COMPLETION CONDITION: SAVEM of a multi-sector range followed by DIR shows an intact directory, and the file loads back with LOADM. MITIGATED 2026-08-28: SD write-back is now gated behind COCO_DSK_WRITEBACK, default 0, so corruption can no longer reach the card. The queue still drains and the dedup still runs - only the f_write is suppressed - and a dropped flush logs '[dsk: N sector(s) NOT written back]'. Behaviour reverts to pre-FRUITJAM-81: saves work within a session and are lost on power-down. Set the flag to 1 once this issue is fixed. DOWNGRADED 2026-08-28 - DID NOT REPRODUCE, and the original diagnosis was probably wrong. Follow-up on hardware: larger SAVEM writes (8 KB+, far more sectors than the 512-byte screen save that triggered the report) completed fine, and after a reboot DIR is CLEAN. That second fact is the important one: a reboot reloads the image from SD, so a clean DIR means the ON-CARD image was never damaged - the sectors written back at 12:35 were good. So the 'garbage' was transient, confined to the PSRAM copy or to the display, and 'write-back made a latent bug permanent' - the reasoning that made this high priority - does not hold. WHAT WAS ACTUALLY OBSERVED: one DIR returning garbage, once, immediately after SAVEM"SCREEN",&H400,&H5FF,&H400. Note that command saves the TEXT SCREEN ITSELF while RSDOS is writing to it, so the saved content is self-modifying by construction; that may explain an odd result without any emulation fault. It was filed as high-severity data corruption on that single observation, which was too strong. STILL WORTH KEEPING OPEN: a garbage DIR is not normal and nothing has explained it. If it recurs, capture whether DIR is garbage again after a REBOOT (on-disk) or only before one (in-memory) - that single check separates a real FDC fault from a transient. Reproducing it needs a human at the keyboard today, which is why FRUITJAM-89 (serial console) would help. Priority high -> low.

summary: Serial console: type into the emulated machine over USB CDC
description: This port has ZERO serial input - not one Serial.read() in src/. The CDC link is output-only, so the only way to type into the machine is a USB HID keyboard. PRIOR ART EXISTS: the sibling AMOLED port implements one and documents it in docs/SERIAL-CONSOLE.md. Its framing is the right one and worth repeating - 'the vendored XRoar core has no serial interface. Nothing in lib/xroar_core or lib/coco_machine touches the UART... the entire adapter is bespoke code, and it is a HOST console, not a machine peripheral.' So this is not an extraction job; it is port glue, with a working implementation next door to crib from. WHY IT IS WORTH HAVING: (1) testing without a keyboard attached - FRUITJAM-88 needs SAVEM reproductions typed repeatedly, and each one currently requires a human at the board; (2) it makes the no-keyboard path debuggable, which is the path the buttons exist for; (3) it would let an agent drive test sequences directly rather than dictating them. IMPLEMENTATION NOTES for whoever does it: reuse the existing ASCII-to-DSCAN mapping and the autotype state machine from FRUITJAM-72 (dscan_for() and autotype_task() already handle key hold and gap timing against the ROM's matrix polling, including SHIFT for characters like quote) - a serial console is essentially autotype with a different source of characters. Feed bytes from Serial into g_type_buf rather than duplicating the key injection. WATCH: the read must be non-blocking and guarded the same way the writes are (availableForWrite is already used everywhere to avoid a connected-but-not-draining host stalling core 0 - the FRUITJAM-35 freeze suspect); the same care applies in reverse. Also decide whether host keys should be swallowed while the picker overlay is modal, as USB keys are. COMPLETION CONDITION: typing in a serial terminal reaches BASIC, and a multi-line paste (a short program plus RUN) arrives intact.

summary: Use the onboard ESP32-C6: networked disk images, remote console, OTA
description: The Fruit Jam carries an ESP32-C6 co-processor that this port does not touch at all. HARDWARE, from the adafruit_fruitjam variant: SerialESP32 is Serial1 on GPIO8 TX / GPIO9 RX; SPIWIFI is SPI1 with SPIWIFI_SS on GPIO46 and SPIWIFI_ACK (BUSY/READY) on GPIO3; ESP32_RESETN is PIN_PERIPHERAL_RESET and ESP32_GPIO0 is PIN_I2S_IRQ. That last pair matters - holding GPIO0 low across a reset puts the C6 in its bootloader, so the RP2350 can REFLASH it. We are not stuck with whatever firmware ships. The SS/ACK arrangement is the classic Adafruit AirLift / nina-fw shape, so WiFiNINA-style firmware is the obvious starting point. WHAT IT UNLOCKS, in order of fit with this project: (1) DISK IMAGES OVER THE NETWORK - no card swapping, and done in OUR overlay idiom rather than a separate configuration application. FRUITJAM-81's design principle applies directly: browse remote images in the same VDG-font 32x16 list, so it still reads as part of the machine. FujiNet is the named counter-example. (2) REMOTE CONSOLE - FRUITJAM-89 with a longer cable. (3) OTA FIRMWARE UPDATE, given RESETN/GPIO0 access. (4) TIME AND DATE, which a CoCo never had without a cartridge. A networked CoCo sits squarely in the 'machine that should have existed' line this port is following. POWER, recorded as a known risk rather than a blocker - the user has accepted it: FRUITJAM-53 measured the desync rate tracking board current, ~21/hr with ~100 mA of LED strip lit against ~5.9/hr dark, roughly 3.5x. WiFi transmit bursts are 200-350 mA transients on the same rail, plus RF energy beside a marginal TMDS link. Supply capacity is not the concern under development (powered from an M4 MacBook Pro port); transient response and decoupling are, and a field deployment on a phone charger would be a different case worth re-checking. SILVER LINING: this is the cleanest available experiment for whether rail loading is the FRUITJAM-58 onset mechanism - a controllable, repeatable current transient on demand. Instrument the desync rate against radio activity from the start. COMPLETION CONDITION: the C6 is brought up and something useful crosses the link - fetching a .dsk over the network is the target - with the desync rate measured against the 7.6/hr baseline.
